title: I. Father Ferapont
paragraphs: Alyosha was woken early, before daybreak. Father Zosima had woken up feeling very weak, though he wanted to get out of bed and sit up in a chair. His mind was completely clear; his face looked tired but bright, almost joyful. It wore an expression of good humor, kindness, and warmth. "I may not live through the coming day," he told Alyosha. Then he asked to confess and take communion right away. He always confessed to Father Paissy. After taking communion, he received the rite of extreme unction. The monks gathered, and the cell gradually filled with people from the hermitage. By now it was daylight. People began arriving from the monastery. When the service ended, the elder wanted to kiss and say goodbye to everyone. Since the cell was so small, the earlier visitors stepped out to make room for others. Alyosha stood beside the elder, who had been settled back into his armchair. He talked as much as he could. His voice was weak but fairly steady.

"I've been teaching you for so many years, and talking out loud for so many years, that I've fallen into the habit of talking—so much so that it's harder for me to hold my tongue than to speak, even now, weak as I am, dear fathers and brothers," he joked, looking with emotion at the group around him.

Alyosha remembered parts of what he said afterward. Though he spoke clearly and his voice held fairly steady, his speech wandered. He touched on many things—he seemed anxious, before the moment of death, to say everything he hadn't managed to say in his life, and not simply to instruct them, but as if he were thirsting to share his joy and ecstasy with everyone and everything alive, and to open his whole heart once more before he died.

"Love one another, fathers," Father Zosima said, as far as Alyosha could recall afterward. "Love God's people. We are not holier than those outside these walls simply because we've come here and shut ourselves in—on the contrary, the very act of coming here means each of us has admitted to himself that he is worse than others, worse than everyone on earth.... And the longer a monk lives in seclusion, the more sharply he has to recognize that. Otherwise he'd have had no reason to come here at all. Only when he understands that he is not merely worse than others, but that he is answerable to everyone for everyone and for everything—for all human sins, of nations and of individuals alike—only then is the purpose of our seclusion fulfilled. Know this, dear ones: every one of us is unquestionably responsible for all people and everything on earth, not just through the general sinfulness of creation, but personally, each of us, for all mankind and every individual person. This knowledge is the crown of life for a monk, and for every human being. Monks aren't a special breed of people—they're simply what every person ought to be. Only through that knowledge does the heart soften into infinite, universal, inexhaustible love. Then every one of you will have the power to win over the whole world with love, and to wash away the world's sins with your tears.... Each of you, watch over your own heart, and confess your sins to yourself without ceasing. Don't be afraid of your sins, even once you recognize them, as long as there is repentance—but don't bargain with God. I say again: don't be proud. Be proud neither toward the small nor toward the great. Don't hate those who reject you, who insult you, who abuse and slander you. Don't hate the atheists, the teachers of evil, the materialists—and I don't just mean the good ones among them, though there are many good ones, especially nowadays—don't hate even the wicked ones. Remember them in your prayers, saying: Save, O Lord, all those who have no one to pray for them, and save too those who will not pray. And add: it is not out of pride that I offer this prayer, O Lord, for I am lower than everyone.... Love God's people, and don't let strangers lead the flock astray, for if you doze off in laziness and contemptuous pride, or worse, in greed, they will come from every direction and lead your flock away. Explain the Gospel to the people without ceasing... don't be greedy for money.... Don't love gold and silver, don't hoard it.... Have faith. Hold to the banner and raise it high."

But the elder's speech was more disjointed than Alyosha's later account of it. Sometimes he broke off entirely, as if to catch his breath and gather his strength, but he was in a kind of ecstasy. They listened with emotion, though many were puzzled by his words and found them obscure.... Afterward everyone remembered those words.

When Alyosha stepped out of the cell for a moment, he was struck by the general excitement and tension among the monks crowding around it. In some it showed as anxiety, in others as solemn devotion. Everyone was expecting some kind of marvel to happen the instant the elder died. The suspense was, in a way, almost frivolous, but even the sternest of the monks were caught up in it. Father Paissy's face looked the gravest of all.

Alyosha was quietly called away by a monk to see Rakitin, who had come from town with a strange letter for him from Madame Khokhlakov. In it she told Alyosha about a strange and remarkably well-timed incident. Among the women who had come the previous day to receive Father Zosima's blessing, there had been an old woman from town, a sergeant's widow named Prokhorovna. She had asked whether she might pray for the soul of her son Vasenka, who had gone off to Irkutsk and hadn't written in over a year. Father Zosima had answered her sternly, forbidding it, saying that praying for the living as if they were dead was a kind of sorcery. Afterward he had forgiven her for her ignorance and added, "as if reading from the book of the future" (this was Madame Khokhlakov's phrase), words of comfort: that her son Vasya was certainly alive, and would either come himself very soon or send a letter, and that she should go home and wait for him. "And would you believe it?" Madame Khokhlakov exclaimed enthusiastically, "the prophecy has come true, literally—and more than that." The old woman had barely gotten home when they handed her a letter from Siberia that had been waiting for her. But that wasn't all: in the letter, written on the road from Yekaterinburg, Vasya told his mother he was returning to Russia with an official, and that three weeks after she received the letter he hoped "to embrace his mother."

Madame Khokhlakov earnestly begged Alyosha to report this new "miracle of prophecy" to the Superior and the whole brotherhood. "Everyone, everyone ought to know of it!" she finished. The letter had been dashed off in a hurry, the writer's excitement showing in every line. But Alyosha didn't need to tell the monks—they already knew. Rakitin had instructed the monk carrying his message "to inform his reverence Father Paissy, most respectfully, that he, Rakitin, has a matter to discuss with him so pressing that he dares not put it off for even a moment, and humbly begs forgiveness for his presumption." Since the monk had delivered the message to Father Paissy before delivering it to Alyosha, Alyosha found, once he'd read the letter, that there was nothing left for him to do but hand it to Father Paissy to confirm the story.
And even that stern, cautious man, though he frowned as he read the news of the "miracle," couldn't entirely suppress some inner emotion. His eyes gleamed, and a grave, solemn smile touched his lips.
"We shall see greater things yet!" broke from him.
"We shall see greater things, greater things yet!" the monks around him repeated.

But Father Paissy, frowning again, asked everyone, at least for now, not to speak of the matter "until it is more fully confirmed, since there is so much credulity in this world, and indeed this might well have happened naturally," he added cautiously, as if to satisfy his own conscience, though he clearly didn't quite believe his own disclaimer—and his listeners could see it just as clearly.

Within the hour the "miracle" was, of course, known throughout the monastery, and to many of the visitors who had come for the mass. No one seemed more struck by it than the monk who had arrived the day before from St. Sylvester's, the small monastery of Obdorsk in the far north. He was the one who had been standing near Madame Khokhlakov the day before and had earnestly asked Father Zosima, about the "healing" of the lady's daughter, "How can you presume to do such things?"

Now he was rather at a loss, unsure whom to believe. The evening before, he had visited Father Ferapont in his cell off by himself, behind the apiary, and had come away deeply impressed and awed by the visit. This Father Ferapont was the aged monk, mentioned earlier, so rigorous in fasting and keeping silence, who was hostile to Father Zosima and to the whole institution of "elders," which he regarded as a harmful and frivolous innovation. He was a formidable opponent, even though his habit of silence meant he barely spoke a word to anyone. What made him formidable was that a number of monks fully shared his feelings, and many visitors regarded him as a great saint and ascetic, even though they had no doubt he was mad. But it was precisely his madness that drew them to him.

Father Ferapont never visited the elder. Though he lived in the hermitage, no one pressed him to keep its rules, largely because he behaved as though he were mad. He was seventy-five or older, and lived in a corner beyond the apiary, in an old, decaying wooden cell that had been built long ago for another great ascetic, Father Iona, who had lived to a hundred and five, and about whose saintly doings many odd stories still circulated in the monastery and the surrounding area.

Father Ferapont had managed to get himself installed in this same isolated cell seven years earlier. It was really just a peasant's hut, though it looked like a chapel, since it held an extraordinary number of icons, with lamps burning before them perpetually—icons that people had brought to the monastery as offerings to God. Father Ferapont had been assigned to look after them and keep the lamps lit. It was said—and it was true—that he ate only two pounds of bread every three days. The beekeeper, who lived close to the apiary, brought him bread every three days, and even to this man who waited on him, Father Ferapont rarely said a word. The four pounds of bread, along with the sacramental bread the Father Superior regularly sent him after the late mass on Sundays, made up his weekly rations. The water in his jug was changed daily. He rarely appeared at mass. Visitors who came to pay him homage sometimes found him kneeling all day in prayer without so much as glancing around. If he spoke to them at all, it was brief, abrupt, strange, and almost always rude. On very rare occasions he would talk with visitors, but usually he would just utter some strange saying that was a complete riddle, and no amount of pleading could get him to explain it. He was not a priest, only a simple monk. There was a strange belief, mostly among the more ignorant, that Father Ferapont communed with heavenly spirits and would only speak with them, which was why he stayed silent with men.

The monk from Obdorsk, directed to the apiary by the beekeeper—himself a very silent and surly monk—went to the corner where Father Ferapont's cell stood. "He might talk to you, being a stranger, or you might get nothing out of him at all," the beekeeper had warned him. The monk, as he related afterward, approached in a state of considerable apprehension. It was fairly late in the evening. Father Ferapont was sitting on a low bench at the door of his cell. A huge old elm rustled softly overhead. There was an evening chill in the air. The monk from Obdorsk bowed low before the saint and asked for his blessing.
"You want me to bow to you, monk?" said Father Ferapont. "Get up!"
The monk got up.
"Blessing—be blessed! Sit beside me. Where have you come from?"

What struck the poor monk most was that, despite his strict fasting and great age, Father Ferapont still looked a vigorous old man. He was tall, stood erect, and had a thin but fresh, healthy face. There was no doubt he still had considerable strength. He was built like an athlete. Despite his great age he wasn't even fully gray, and still had thick hair and a full beard, both once black. His eyes were gray, large, and bright, but strikingly bulging. He spoke with a broad, rustic accent. He wore a peasant's long, reddish coat of coarse convict cloth, as it used to be called, with a thick rope tied round his waist. His throat and chest were bare. Under the coat, his shirt of the coarsest linen showed nearly black with dirt, not having been changed in months. People said he wore chains weighing thirty pounds under his coat. His bare feet, without stockings, were shoved into old slippers that were nearly falling apart.
"From the little Obdorsk monastery, from St. Sylvester's," the monk answered humbly, his sharp, curious, but rather frightened little eyes fixed on the hermit.
"I've stayed at your Sylvester's. I used to lodge there. Is Sylvester keeping well?"
The monk hesitated.
"You're a senseless lot! How do you keep your fasts?"

"Our diet follows the old conventual rules. During Lent there are no meals provided on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays. On Tuesdays and Thursdays we have white bread, stewed fruit with honey, wild berries, or salted cabbage and wholemeal porridge. On Saturdays, white cabbage soup, noodles with peas, kasha, all with hemp oil. On weekdays we have dried fish with kasha and cabbage soup. From Monday through Saturday evening—six full days of Holy Week—nothing is cooked, and we have only bread and water, sparingly at that, and if possible we don't eat every day, just as is prescribed for the first week of Lent. On Good Friday nothing is eaten at all. Likewise on Holy Saturday we fast until three o'clock, then take a little bread and water and a single cup of wine. On Holy Thursday we drink wine and eat something cooked without oil, or nothing cooked at all, since the Council of Laodicea lays down for Holy Thursday: 'It is unseemly, by relaxing the fast on Holy Thursday, to dishonor the whole of Lent!' That's how we keep the fast. But what is that compared to you, holy father," the monk added, growing bolder, "since all year round, even at Easter, you take nothing but bread and water, and what we eat in two days lasts you a full week. It's truly marvelous—your great abstinence."
"And mushrooms?" Father Ferapont asked suddenly.
"Mushrooms?" the monk repeated, surprised.

"Yes. I can do without their bread—I don't need it at all—and go off into the forest and live there on mushrooms or berries, but they can't give up their bread here, and so they're in bondage to the devil. Nowadays the unclean claim there's no need for such fasting. Their judgment is arrogant and unclean."
"Ah, true," the monk sighed.
"And have you seen devils among them?" Ferapont asked.
"Among them? Among whom?" the monk asked timidly.

"I went to see the Father Superior last Trinity Sunday, I haven't been since. I saw a devil sitting on one man's chest, hiding under his cassock, only his horns poking out; another had one peeking out of his pocket, with such sharp eyes—he was afraid of me; another had settled in the unclean belly of one man; another was hanging round a man's neck, so that he carried him about without knowing it."
"You—can see spirits?" the monk asked.

"I tell you I can see, I can see straight through them. When I was leaving the Superior's, I saw one hiding from me behind the door—a big one, a yard and a half tall or more, with a thick, long gray tail, and the tip of his tail was caught in the crack of the door, and I was quick and slammed the door on it, pinching his tail. He squealed and started struggling, and I made the sign of the cross over him three times. And he died on the spot, like a crushed spider. He must have rotted there in the corner and be stinking by now, but they don't see it, they don't smell it. It's been a year since I've been there. I'm telling you this because you're a stranger."

"Your words are terrible! But, holy and blessed father," the monk said, growing bolder and bolder, "is it true, as people say even in distant lands, that you are in constant communication with the Holy Ghost?"
"He does fly down sometimes."
"How does he fly down? In what form?"
"As a bird."
"The Holy Ghost in the form of a dove?"
"There's the Holy Ghost and there's the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit can appear as other birds too—sometimes a swallow, sometimes a goldfinch, sometimes a blue tit."
"How do you tell him apart from an ordinary tit?"
"He speaks."
"How does he speak—in what language?"
"Human language."
"And what does he tell you?"
"Why, today he told me a fool would come to visit me and ask unseemly questions. You want to know too much, monk."
"Your words are terrible, most holy and blessed father," the monk said, shaking his head. But there was a doubtful look in his frightened little eyes.
"Do you see that tree?" Father Ferapont asked, after a pause.
"I do, blessed father."
"You think it's an elm, but to me it has another shape."
"What shape?" the monk asked, after waiting in vain for more.
"It happens at night. You see those two branches? At night it's Christ holding out His arms to me and reaching for me with them, I see it clearly and I tremble. It's terrible, terrible!"
"What's terrible about it, if it's Christ Himself?"
"Why, He'll snatch me up and carry me off."
"Alive?"
"In the spirit and glory of Elijah—haven't you heard? He'll take me in His arms and bear me away."

Though the monk went back to the cell he shared with one of the brothers in considerable confusion of mind, he still felt, at heart, a greater reverence for Father Ferapont than for Father Zosima. He was strongly in favor of fasting, and it seemed to him not at all strange that a man who kept so rigorous a fast as Father Ferapont should "see marvels." His words certainly sounded odd, but God alone could know what was hidden in those words, and weren't stranger words and deeds commonly seen among those who had sacrificed their intellects for God's glory? He was ready and eager to believe in the pinching of the devil's tail, and not only in some figurative sense. Besides, before visiting the monastery he had already held a strong prejudice against the institution of "elders," which he knew only by hearsay and believed to be a harmful innovation. He hadn't been at the monastery long before he'd picked up on the muttered complaints of some shallow brothers who disliked the practice. He was, besides, a meddlesome, nosy man who poked into everything. This was why the news of Father Zosima's fresh "miracle" left him thoroughly perplexed. Alyosha remembered afterward how their curious guest from Obdorsk had kept flitting from one group to another, listening and asking questions among the monks crowding inside and outside the elder's cell. But he hadn't paid him much attention at the time, and only remembered it later.

In fact, he had no attention to spare for it, because when Father Zosima, feeling tired again, had gone back to bed, he thought of Alyosha as he was closing his eyes, and sent for him. Alyosha ran at once. No one else was in the cell but Father Paissy, Father Iosif, and the novice Porfiry. The elder opened his weary eyes, looked intently at Alyosha, and asked him suddenly:
"Are your people expecting you, my son?"
Alyosha hesitated.
"Don't they need you? Didn't you promise someone yesterday that you'd see them today?"
"I did promise—my father—my brothers—others too."

"You see, then, you must go. Don't grieve. Rest assured I won't die without you at my side to hear my last word. That word I'll say to you, my son—it will be my last gift to you. To you, dear son, because you love me. But now go and keep your promise."

Alyosha obeyed at once, though it was hard to leave. But the promise that he would hear the elder's last word on earth, that it would be his last gift to him, Alyosha, sent a thrill of rapture through his soul. He hurried so he could finish what he had to do in town and come back quickly. Father Paissy, too, spoke some words of exhortation that moved and surprised him greatly. He spoke them as they left the cell together.

"Remember, young man, and never forget," Father Paissy began, without preamble, "that the science of this world, which has become a great power, has, especially in the last century, analyzed everything divine handed down to us in the holy books. After this ruthless analysis, the learned men of this world have nothing left of all that was once sacred. But they've only analyzed the parts and overlooked the whole, and their blindness is truly astonishing. Yet the whole still stands firm before their eyes, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. Hasn't it lasted nineteen centuries? Isn't it still a living, moving power in the individual soul and in the masses of people? It remains just as strong and alive even in the souls of atheists who have torn everything else down! For even those who have renounced Christianity and attack it still, in their innermost being, follow the Christian ideal—because neither their cleverness nor the fervor of their hearts has yet managed to create a higher ideal of man and of virtue than the one Christ gave long ago. Whenever they've tried, the result has only been grotesque. Remember this above all, young man, since your dying elder is sending you out into the world. Perhaps, remembering this great day, you won't forget these words of mine, spoken from the heart to guide you, since you are young and the world's temptations are great and beyond your strength to bear. Now go, my orphan."

With these words Father Paissy blessed him. As Alyosha left the monastery and turned them over in his mind, he suddenly realized he had found a new and unexpected friend, a warmly loving teacher, in this stern monk who had always treated him so severely before. It was as though Father Zosima had bequeathed him to Father Paissy on his deathbed, and "maybe that's exactly what passed between them," Alyosha thought suddenly. The philosophical reflections he'd just heard so unexpectedly testified to the warmth of Father Paissy's heart. He was in a hurry to arm the boy's mind for the coming struggle with temptation, and to guard the young soul left in his charge with the strongest defense he could think of.

title: II. At His Father's
paragraphs: First, Alyosha went to see his father. On the way he remembered that his father had insisted the day before that he come without letting his brother Ivan see him. "Why is that?" Alyosha wondered suddenly. "Even if father has something to tell me privately, why do I need to sneak in unseen? He probably meant something different, worked up as he was yesterday," he decided. Still, he was glad when Marfa Ignatyevna, who opened the garden gate for him (Grigory, it turned out, was laid up sick in the lodge), told him, in answer to his question, that Ivan Fyodorovitch had gone out two hours earlier.
"And my father?"
"He's up, having his coffee," Marfa answered, somewhat dryly.

Alyosha went in. The old man was sitting alone at the table, in slippers and an old overcoat, looking over some accounts, rather absentmindedly. He was completely alone in the house, since Smerdyakov too had gone out marketing. Although he'd gotten up early and was trying to put on a brave face, he looked tired and worn out. His forehead, where huge purple bruises had come up overnight, was wrapped in a red handkerchief; his nose, too, had swollen badly overnight, patched with smaller bruises, giving his whole face a peculiarly spiteful, irritable look. The old man knew it, and shot Alyosha a hostile glance as he came in.
"The coffee's cold," he snapped. "I won't offer you any. I've ordered nothing but a Lenten fish soup today, and I'm not inviting anyone to share it. Why have you come?"
"To see how you are," said Alyosha.
"Yes. Besides, I told you to come yesterday. None of it matters. You needn't have bothered. But I knew you'd come poking in anyway."

He said this with an almost hostile edge. At the same time he got up and anxiously checked his nose in the mirror—probably for the fortieth time that morning. He also started tying his red handkerchief more neatly around his forehead.
"Red suits better. White makes it look like a hospital," he observed sententiously. "Well, how are things over there? How's your elder?"
"He's very bad—he may die today," Alyosha answered. But his father wasn't listening, and had already forgotten his own question.

"Ivan's gone out," he said suddenly. "He's doing everything he can to steal Mitya's fiancée away. That's why he's still hanging around here," he added spitefully, twisting his mouth as he looked at Alyosha.
"He didn't actually tell you that, did he?" Alyosha asked.
"Yes, he did, ages ago. Would you believe it, he told me three weeks back? You don't suppose he came here to murder me too, do you? He must have had some reason for coming."
"What do you mean? Why would you say such a thing?" said Alyosha, troubled.

"He doesn't ask me for money, it's true, but he won't get a farthing out of me either way. I intend to live as long as I possibly can, you may as well know that, my dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, so I need every farthing, and the longer I live, the more I'll need," he went on, pacing from one corner of the room to the other, hands stuffed in the pockets of his loose, greasy yellow cotton overcoat. "I can still pass for a man in his fifties, but I want to keep passing for one another twenty years. As I get older, you know, I won't be much to look at. The girls won't come to me on their own, so I'll need my money. So I'm saving up more and more, purely for myself, my dear son Alexey Fyodorovitch. You might as well know it. Because I intend to keep sinning right to the end, let me tell you. Sin is sweet—everyone denounces it, but everyone lives in it; the difference is that others do it on the sly, and I do it out in the open. And that's why all the other sinners come after me—for being so honest about it. And your paradise, Alexey Fyodorovitch, isn't to my taste, let me tell you that; it's no place for a gentleman, that paradise of yours, even if it exists. My belief is that I'll fall asleep and never wake up, and that's the end of it. Pray for my soul if you want. And if you don't want to, don't, damn you! That's my philosophy. Ivan talked well here yesterday, even drunk as we all were. Ivan's a conceited popinjay, but he hasn't got any real learning... or education either. He just sits there silent, smiling without saying anything—that's what gets him through."
Alyosha listened to him in silence.

"Why won't he talk to me? When he does speak, he puts on airs. Your Ivan is a scoundrel! And I'll marry Grushenka this minute if I feel like it. Because if you've got money, Alexey Fyodorovitch, all you have to do is want a thing and you can have it. That's what Ivan's afraid of—he's watching to stop me from marrying, which is why he's egging Mitya on to marry Grushenka himself. He thinks that'll keep me away from Grushenka (as if I'd leave him my money if I don't marry her!). Besides, if Mitya marries Grushenka, Ivan gets to run off with his rich fiancée—that's what he's counting on! He's a scoundrel, your Ivan!"
"You're so bad-tempered! It's from yesterday—you should lie down," said Alyosha.

"There—you say that," the old man observed suddenly, as though it had just struck him, "and I'm not angry with you. But if Ivan said it, I'd be furious with him. It's only with you that I have good moments—otherwise, you know, I'm a nasty man."
"You're not nasty, just twisted," said Alyosha with a smile.

"Listen. This morning I meant to have that ruffian Mitya locked up, and now I don't know what I'll decide about it. Of course, in these fashionable times, fathers and mothers are treated like a prejudice, but even now the law doesn't let you drag your old father around by the hair, kick him in the face in his own house, and brag about killing him outright—all in front of witnesses. If I wanted, I could crush him, and I could have him locked up right now for what he did yesterday."
"So you don't intend to press charges?"
"Ivan talked me out of it. I wouldn't care about Ivan's opinion, but there's another reason."
And bending toward Alyosha, he went on in a confidential half-whisper.

"If I send that ruffian to prison, she'll hear about it and run straight to see him. But if she hears he's beaten me, a weak old man, half to death, she might give him up and come to me instead.... That's how she is, everything by contraries. I know her through and through! Won't you have a drop of brandy? Take some cold coffee and I'll pour in a quarter glass of brandy—it's delicious, my boy."

"No, thank you. I'll take that roll with me, if I may," said Alyosha, and taking a small French roll, he put it in the pocket of his cassock. "And you'd better skip the brandy too," he suggested cautiously, looking into the old man's face.
"You're quite right, it irritates my nerves instead of soothing them. Just one little glass. I'll get it out of the cupboard."
He unlocked the cupboard, poured out a glass, drank it, then locked the cupboard again and put the key back in his pocket.
"That's enough. One glass won't kill me."
"See, you're in a better mood now," said Alyosha, smiling.

"Hm! I love you even without the brandy, but with scoundrels I'm a scoundrel myself. Ivan's not going to Tchermashnya—why is that? He wants to spy on how much I give Grushenka if she comes. They're all scoundrels! But I don't recognize Ivan, I don't understand him at all. Where does he come from? He's not one of us, not in his soul. As if I'd leave him anything! I'm not going to leave a will at all, you might as well know. And I'll crush Mitya like a beetle. I squash black beetles at night with my slipper—they squelch when you step on them. And your Mitya will squelch too. _Your_ Mitya, since you love him. Yes, you love him, and I'm not afraid of your loving him. But if Ivan loved him, I'd be afraid of myself over it. But Ivan doesn't love anybody. Ivan isn't one of us. People like Ivan aren't our kind, my boy. They're like a cloud of dust. When the wind blows, the dust is gone.... I had a foolish idea in my head when I told you to come today; I wanted to find out from you about Mitya. If I were to hand him a thousand, or maybe two, right now, would the miserable wretch agree to clear off entirely for five years—or better, thirty-five—without Grushenka, and give her up for good, eh?"
"I—I'll ask him," Alyosha muttered. "If you gave him three thousand, maybe he—"

"That's nonsense! No need to ask him now, none at all! I've changed my mind. It was a foolish idea of mine. I won't give him anything, not a penny—I want my money for myself," the old man cried, waving his hand. "I'll crush him like a beetle without it. Don't say a word to him about it or he'll start hoping. There's nothing for you to do here, you don't need to stay. That fiancée of his, Katerina Ivanovna, whom he's kept so carefully hidden from me all this time—is she going to marry him or not? You went to see her yesterday, I believe?"
"Nothing will make her give him up."

"There, you see how dearly these fine young ladies love a rake and a scoundrel. They're pathetic creatures, I tell you, these pale young ladies, very different from—ah, if I had his youth and the looks I had back then (I was better-looking than he is now, at twenty-eight), I'd have been just as much a conquering hero as he is. He's a low cad! But he won't have Grushenka, all the same, he won't! I'll crush him!"
His anger had flared up again with these last words.
"You can go. There's nothing for you to do here today," he snapped harshly.
Alyosha went up to say goodbye and kissed him on the shoulder.
"What's that for?" The old man was a little startled. "We'll see each other again—or don't you think so?"
"Not at all, I didn't mean anything by it."

"Neither did I, I didn't mean anything either," said the old man, looking at him. "Listen, listen," he called after him, "hurry back and I'll have fish soup for you, a good one, not like today's. Be sure to come! Come tomorrow, do you hear, tomorrow!"
And as soon as Alyosha had gone out the door, he went back to the cupboard and poured himself another half-glass.

"I won't have more!" he muttered, clearing his throat, and again he locked the cupboard and put the key in his pocket. Then he went into his bedroom, lay down on the bed, exhausted, and was asleep within a minute.

title: III. A Meeting With The Schoolboys
paragraphs: "Thank goodness he didn't ask about Grushenka," Alyosha thought as he left his father's house and headed toward Madame Khokhlakov's, "or I might have had to tell him about running into Grushenka yesterday."

Alyosha felt painfully aware that since yesterday both combatants had renewed their energy, and their hearts had hardened all over again. "Father is spiteful and angry, he's cooked up some plan and he'll stick to it. And what about Dmitri? He'll be harder than yesterday too, he must be spiteful and angry too, and no doubt he's cooked up some plan of his own. Oh, I have to manage to find him today, no matter what."

But Alyosha didn't have long to think it over. Something happened on the road that, though apparently trivial, made a strong impression on him. Just after he crossed the square and turned the corner onto Mihailovsky Street, which is separated from the High Street by a small ditch (our whole town is crisscrossed with ditches), he saw a group of schoolboys, aged nine to twelve, at the bridge. They were heading home from school, some with bags over their shoulders, others with leather satchels slung across them, some in short jackets, others in little overcoats. A few even wore those tall boots with creased ankles that little boys spoiled by rich fathers love to wear. The whole group was talking eagerly about something, apparently holding a council. Ever since his Moscow days, Alyosha had never been able to walk past children without noticing them, and though he was especially fond of children around three years old, he liked schoolboys of ten or eleven too. So, worried as he was that day, he wanted to stop and talk to them right away. He looked into their excited, rosy faces and noticed at once that every boy had stones in his hands. On the far side of the ditch, some thirty paces off, another schoolboy stood by a fence. He too had a satchel at his side. He looked about ten, pale, delicate, with sparkling black eyes. He kept a watchful, anxious eye on the other six—obviously his schoolmates, whom he'd just walked out of school with, but with whom he'd clearly had a falling-out.
Alyosha went up to a fair-haired, curly-headed, rosy-cheeked boy in a black jacket and remarked:
"When I used to wear a satchel like yours, I always carried it on my left side, to keep my right hand free, but you've got yours on your right side. That'll make it awkward to get at."

Alyosha had no art or forethought in opening with this practical remark. But it's the only way for a grown-up to get straight into a child's confidence—or even more so, a group of children's. You have to start in a serious, businesslike way, so as to meet them on completely equal footing. Alyosha understood this by instinct.
"But he's left-handed," another boy, sturdy and healthy-looking, about eleven, answered promptly. All the others stared at Alyosha.
"He even throws stones with his left hand," a third observed.
At that instant a stone flew into the group, only just grazing the left-handed boy, though it had been thrown well and hard by the boy standing on the other side of the ditch.

"Get him, hit him back, Smurov," they all shouted. But Smurov, the left-handed boy, needed no urging and struck back at once—he threw a stone, but it missed the boy and hit the ground instead. The boy on the other side of the ditch, whose coat pocket was visibly bulging with stones, hurled another at the group; this one flew straight at Alyosha and struck him painfully on the shoulder.

"He aimed it at you, he meant it for you. You're Karamazov, Karamazov!" the boys shouted, laughing. "Come on, all throw at him at once!" and six stones flew at the boy. One hit him on the head and he fell, but immediately leapt up and began fiercely returning fire. Both sides kept up a steady barrage. Many of the boys in the group had their pockets full too.
"What are you doing! Aren't you ashamed? Six against one! You'll kill him!" Alyosha cried.
He ran forward, putting himself in the path of the flying stones to shield the lone boy. Three or four of them stopped throwing for a moment.

"He started it!" a boy in a red shirt cried in an angry, childish voice. "He's a beast, he stabbed Krassotkin in class the other day with a penknife. It bled. Krassotkin wouldn't tell on him, but he ought to get thrashed for it."
"But why? I suppose you tease him."

"There, he's thrown another one at your back, he knows who you are," the children cried. "It's you he's aiming at now, not us. Come on, everyone, at him again, don't miss, Smurov!" and another volley of stones began, an even nastier one. The boy on the other side of the ditch was hit in the chest; he screamed, burst into tears, and ran off uphill toward Mihailovsky Street. They all shouted: "Ha, he's funking it, he's running away. Wisp of tow!"
"You don't know what a beast he is, Karamazov, killing's too good for him," said the boy in the jacket, eyes flashing. He seemed to be the oldest.
"What's wrong with him?" Alyosha asked. "Is he a tattletale, or what?"
The boys glanced at one another, almost mockingly.
"Are you headed that way, to Mihailovsky?" the same boy went on. "Catch up with him.... See, he's stopped again, he's waiting and watching you."
"He's looking at you," the other boys chimed in.
"Ask him—does he like a disheveled wisp of tow? Go on, ask him that!"
A general burst of laughter followed. Alyosha looked at them, and they looked back at him.
"Don't go near him, he'll hurt you," Smurov called out in warning.
"I won't ask him about the wisp of tow, since I gather you tease him with that somehow. But I'll find out from him why you all hate him so much."
"Go on then, find out," the boys cried, laughing.
Alyosha crossed the bridge and walked uphill along the fence, straight toward the boy.
"You'd better watch out," the boys called after him. "He won't be scared of you. He'll stab you in a second, on the sly, just like he did Krassotkin."

The boy waited for him without moving. Coming closer, Alyosha saw facing him a child of about nine. He was an undersized, frail-looking boy with a thin, pale face and large dark eyes that stared at him with hatred. He wore a rather shabby old overcoat that he'd monstrously outgrown, his bare arms sticking out past the sleeves. There was a big patch on the right knee of his trousers, and in his right boot, right at the toe, a big hole in the leather had been carefully blackened with ink. Both pockets of his overcoat sagged with stones. Alyosha stopped two steps in front of him and looked at him questioningly. The boy, seeing at once from Alyosha's eyes that he wasn't going to hit him, became less defiant and spoke first.
"I'm alone, and there are six of them. I'll beat them all, alone!" he said suddenly, eyes flashing.
"I think one of those stones must have hurt you badly," Alyosha observed.
"But I got Smurov on the head!" the boy cried.
"They told me you know me, and that you threw that stone at me on purpose," said Alyosha.
The boy gave him a dark look.
"I don't know you. Do you know me?" Alyosha went on.
"Leave me alone!" the boy cried irritably; but he didn't move, as if he were waiting for something, and there was that same vindictive light in his eyes.
"All right, I'm going," said Alyosha. "I just don't know you, and I'm not teasing you. They told me how they tease you, but I don't want to tease you. Goodbye!"

"Monk in silk trousers!" the boy shouted, following Alyosha with the same vindictive, defiant look, and he threw himself into a defensive crouch, certain that now Alyosha would come at him; but Alyosha just turned, looked at him, and walked away. He hadn't gone three steps before the biggest stone the boy had in his pocket hit him painfully in the back.

"So you'll hit a man from behind! They were telling the truth, then, when they said you attack on the sly," said Alyosha, turning around again. This time the boy hurled a stone savagely straight at Alyosha's face; but Alyosha just had time to shield himself, and the stone struck him on the elbow.
"Aren't you ashamed? What have I ever done to you?" he cried.

The boy waited in silent defiance, sure that now Alyosha would attack him. Seeing that even now he wouldn't, his rage flared up like a small wild animal's; he flew at Alyosha himself, and before Alyosha had time to move, the vicious child had seized his left hand with both of his and bit down on his middle finger. He sank his teeth in and held on for a full ten seconds before letting go. Alyosha cried out in pain and yanked his finger free with all his strength. The child finally let go and backed off to his former distance. Alyosha's finger was badly bitten, right to the bone near the nail; it started bleeding. Alyosha took out his handkerchief and bound it tightly around his injured hand. It took him a full minute to bandage it. The boy stood waiting the whole time. At last Alyosha raised his gentle eyes and looked at him.
"All right," he said, "you see how badly you've bitten me. That's enough, isn't it? Now tell me—what did I do to you?"
The boy stared at him, astonished.

"Even though I don't know you, and this is the first time I've ever seen you," Alyosha went on, just as calmly, "I must have done something to you—you wouldn't have hurt me like this for no reason. So what did I do? How did I wrong you? Tell me."

Instead of answering, the boy burst into loud, tearful sobs and ran off. Alyosha walked slowly after him toward Mihailovsky Street, and for a long while he could see the child still running in the distance, as fast as ever, not turning his head, no doubt still sobbing. He decided he'd track the boy down as soon as he had time, to get to the bottom of this mystery. But just now he had no time to spare.

title: IV. At The Khokhlakovs'
paragraphs: Alyosha soon reached Madame Khokhlakov's house, a handsome two-story stone house, one of the finest in town. Though Madame Khokhlakov spent most of her time on her estate in another province, or in Moscow, where she had a house of her own, she also had a house here, inherited from her ancestors. The estate in our district was the largest of her three, though she'd spent very little time in our province up to now. She ran out to Alyosha in the hall.
"Did you get my letter about the new miracle?" She spoke quickly, nervously.
"Yes."
"Did you show it to everyone? He gave the son back to his mother!"
"He's dying today," said Alyosha.

"I've heard, I know, oh, how I long to talk to you—to you, or someone—about all this. No, to you, to you! And how sorry I am that I can't see him! The whole town is in an uproar, everyone's on edge. But now—do you know Katerina Ivanovna is here right now?"
"Ah, that's lucky," Alyosha exclaimed. "Then I'll see her here. She told me yesterday to be sure to come see her today."

"I know, I know it all. I've heard exactly what happened yesterday—and the appalling behavior of that—creature. It's tragic, and if I'd been in her place I don't know what I would have done. And your brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch, what do you make of him?—my goodness! Alexey Fyodorovitch, I'm forgetting myself, only imagine—your brother is in there with her right now, not that dreadful brother who behaved so shockingly yesterday, but the other one, Ivan Fyodorovitch—he's sitting with her, talking, they're having a serious conversation. If you could only picture what's passing between them right now—it's dreadful, I tell you, it's harrowing, it's like some unbelievable tale of horror. They're both ruining their lives for no reason anyone can see. They both know it, and they both revel in it. I've been watching for you! I've been dying for you to come! It's too much for me, that's the worst of it. I'll tell you all about it in a moment, but first I must mention something else, the most important thing—I'd completely forgotten the most important thing. Tell me, why has Lise been having hysterics? The moment she heard you were here, she started up!"

"_Maman_, it's you who are hysterical now, not me," Lise's voice sang out through a tiny crack in the door to the side. Her voice sounded as though she wanted to laugh but was doing everything she could to hold it in. Alyosha noticed the crack at once, and Lise was no doubt peeping through it, though he couldn't see that.

"And no wonder, Lise, no wonder... your whims will drive me hysterical too. But she's been so ill, Alexey Fyodorovitch, so ill all night, feverish and moaning! I could barely wait for morning and for Herzenstube to come. He says he can't make anything of it, that we have to wait. Herzenstube always comes and says he can't make anything of it. The moment you came near the house, she screamed, fell into hysterics, and insisted on being wheeled back into this room."
"Mamma, I didn't know he'd come. It wasn't on his account that I wanted to be wheeled into this room."
"That's not true, Lise, Yulia ran to tell you Alexey Fyodorovitch was coming. You'd been watching for him."

"My darling mamma, that's not very clever of you. But if you want to make up for it and say something truly clever, dear mamma, you'd better tell our honored guest, Alexey Fyodorovitch, that he's shown a real lack of sense by daring to show his face here after what happened yesterday, when everyone's laughing at him."

"Lise, you're going too far. I swear I'll have to be strict with you. Who's laughing at him? I'm so glad he's come, I need him, I can't do without him. Oh, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I am exceedingly unhappy!"
"But what's wrong with you, mamma darling?"

"Ah, your whims, Lise, your restlessness, your illness, that awful feverish night, that awful, endless Herzenstube—endless, endless, that's the worst of it! Everything, really, everything.... Even that miracle, too! Oh, how it's upset me, how it's shattered me, that miracle, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch! And that tragedy in the drawing room—it's more than I can bear, I warn you. I can't bear it. A comedy, maybe, not a tragedy. Tell me, will Father Zosima live until tomorrow, will he? Oh, my God! What's happening to me? Every minute I close my eyes and see that it's all nonsense, all nonsense."
"I'd be very grateful," Alyosha suddenly cut in, "if you could give me a clean rag to bind up my finger with. I've hurt it, and it's quite painful."
Alyosha unwrapped his bitten finger. The handkerchief was soaked with blood. Madame Khokhlakov screamed and shut her eyes.
"Good heavens, what a wound, how awful!"
But the moment Lise saw Alyosha's finger through the crack, she flung the door wide open.

"Come here, come here," she cried imperiously. "No nonsense now! Good heavens, why were you just standing there saying nothing about it all this time? He might have bled to death, mamma! How did you do it? Water, water! You must wash it first, just hold it in cold water to stop the pain, and keep it there, keep it there.... Hurry, mamma, some water in a basin. Do hurry," she finished nervously. She was quite frightened at the sight of Alyosha's wound.
"Shouldn't we send for Herzenstube?" cried Madame Khokhlakov.

"Mamma, you'll be the death of me. Your Herzenstube will come and say he can't make anything of it! Water, water! Mamma, for goodness' sake go yourself and hurry Yulia along, she's such a slowpoke and never manages to come quickly! Hurry, mamma, or I'll die."
"It's really nothing much," Alyosha cried, alarmed by all this fuss.
Yulia ran in with water and Alyosha put his finger into it.

"Some lint, mamma, for mercy's sake, bring the lint and that murky caustic lotion for wounds, what's it called? We have some. You know where the bottle is, mamma, it's in your bedroom in the right-hand cupboard, there's a big bottle of it there with the lint."
"I'll bring everything in a minute, Lise, only don't scream and don't fuss. See how bravely Alexey Fyodorovitch is bearing it. Where did you get such a dreadful wound, Alexey Fyodorovitch?"
Madame Khokhlakov hurried off. This was exactly what Lise had been waiting for.
"First, answer the question—where did you get hurt like this?" she asked Alyosha quickly. "And then I'll talk to you about something entirely different. Well?"

Sensing instinctively that her mother's absence was precious time, Alyosha hurried to tell her, in as few words as possible, about his puzzling encounter with the schoolboys. Lise clasped her hands at his story.

"How can you, dressed like that, go around with schoolboys?" she cried angrily, as though she had every right to order him about. "You're nothing but a boy yourself if you do that, a perfect boy! But you must find out about that horrid boy for me and tell me everything, because there's some mystery in it. Now, the second thing—but first a question: does the pain stop you from talking about things that don't matter, but talking sensibly?"
"Of course not, and I don't feel much pain now."

"That's because your finger is in the water. It has to be changed right away, it'll warm up in a minute. Yulia, bring some ice from the cellar and another basin of water. Now that she's gone, I can talk—will you give me back the letter I sent you yesterday, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch—quickly, because mamma will be back any minute and I don't want—"
"I don't have the letter with me."
"That's not true, you do. I knew you'd say that. You've got it in that pocket. I've regretted that joke all night. Give me back the letter right now, give it to me."
"I left it at home."

"But you can't possibly still think of me as a child, a little girl, after that foolish joke! I apologize for that foolishness, but you have to bring me the letter, if you really don't have it—bring it today, you must, you must."
"Today I simply can't, because I'm going back to the monastery and I won't come see you for the next two days—three or four, maybe—because of Father Zosima—"
"Four days, what nonsense! Listen. Did you laugh at me a lot?"
"I didn't laugh at all."
"Why not?"
"Because I believed everything you wrote."
"You're insulting me!"

"Not at all. As soon as I read it, I thought that all of it would come true—because as soon as Father Zosima dies, I'm to leave the monastery. Then I'll go back and finish my studies, and when you come of age, we'll get married. I'll love you. I haven't had time to really think it through, but I believe I couldn't find a better wife than you, and Father Zosima tells me I must marry."
"But I'm a cripple, wheeled around in a chair," Lise laughed, blushing crimson.
"I'll wheel you around myself, but I'm sure you'll be well by then."

"But you're out of your mind," said Lise, nervously, "turning a joke into all this nonsense! Here comes mamma, quite conveniently, perhaps. Mamma, you're always so slow, how can it take you this long! And here's Yulia with the ice!"

"Oh, Lise, don't scream, whatever you do, don't scream. That scream drives me... how can I help it when you put the lint somewhere else? I've been hunting and hunting for it—I really believe you did it on purpose."
"But I couldn't have known he'd show up with a hurt finger, or else maybe I would have done it on purpose. My darling mamma, you're starting to say genuinely witty things."

"Never mind my being witty, but I must say you show a lot of concern for Alexey Fyodorovitch's suffering! Oh, my dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, what's killing me isn't any one thing in particular, not Herzenstube, but everything together, that's what's too much for me."

"That's enough, mamma, enough about Herzenstube," Lise laughed merrily. "Hurry up with the lint and the lotion, mamma. That's just Goulard water, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I remember the name now, but it's a wonderful lotion. Would you believe it, mamma, on his way here he got into a fight with some boys in the street, and one of them bit his finger—isn't he just a child, a perfect child himself? Is he fit to be married after that? Just imagine, he wants to get married, mamma. Just picture him married, wouldn't that be funny, wouldn't that be awful?"
And Lise kept up her thin, hysterical giggle, glancing slyly at Alyosha.
"But why married, Lise? What makes you bring up such a thing? It's completely out of place—and maybe the boy had rabies."
"Oh, mamma! As if there were such things as rabid boys!"

"Why not, Lise, as if I'd said something stupid! Your boy could have been bitten by a mad dog and gone rabid himself and bitten whoever was nearby. How neatly she's bandaged it, Alexey Fyodorovitch! I couldn't have done it. Do you still feel the pain?"
"It's nothing much now."
"You're not afraid of water, are you?" asked Lise.

"Come, that's enough, Lise, maybe I really was a bit too quick talking about the boy having rabies, and you pounced on it right away. Katerina Ivanovna just heard you were here, Alexey Fyodorovitch, she simply flew at me, she's dying to see you, dying!"
"Ach, mamma, go to them yourself. He can't go right now, he's in too much pain."
"Not at all, I can go perfectly well," said Alyosha.
"What! You're leaving? Is that what you're saying?"

"Well, once I've seen them, I'll come back here and we can talk as long as you like. But I'd like to see Katerina Ivanovna right away, because I'm very eager to get back to the monastery as soon as I can."

"Mamma, take him away quickly. Alexey Fyodorovitch, don't bother coming back to see me afterward, just go straight back to your monastery, and good riddance. I want to sleep, I didn't sleep all night."
"Ah, Lise, you're only joking, but how I wish you would sleep!" Madame Khokhlakov cried.
"I don't know what I've done.... I'll stay another three minutes, five if you like," Alyosha muttered.
"Even five! Take him away quickly, mamma, he's a monster."

"Lise, you're being impossible. Let's go, Alexey Fyodorovitch, she's very moody today. I'm afraid to cross her. Oh, the trouble one has with nervous girls! Maybe she really will be able to sleep after seeing you. How quickly you've made her sleepy, and how fortunate that is!"
"Ah, mamma, how sweetly you talk! I have to kiss you for that, mamma."

"And I'll kiss you too, Lise. Listen, Alexey Fyodorovitch," Madame Khokhlakov began, mysteriously and importantly, in a rapid whisper. "I don't want to suggest anything, I don't want to lift the veil, you'll see for yourself what's going on. It's appalling. It's the most fantastic farce. She loves your brother Ivan, and she's doing everything she can to convince herself she loves your brother Dmitri. It's appalling! I'll go in with you, and if they don't throw me out, I'll stay to the end."

title: V. A Laceration In The Drawing-Room
paragraphs: But in the drawing room the conversation had already ended. Katerina Ivanovna was highly agitated, though she looked resolute. Just as Alyosha and Madame Khokhlakov came in, Ivan Fyodorovitch stood up to leave. His face was rather pale, and Alyosha looked at him anxiously. Because this moment was about to settle a doubt, a nagging riddle that had haunted Alyosha for some time now. Over the past month it had been suggested to him several times that his brother Ivan was in love with Katerina Ivanovna, and, what's more, that he meant "to carry her off" from Dmitri. Until quite recently the idea had seemed monstrous to Alyosha, though it troubled him enormously. He loved both his brothers and dreaded any such rivalry between them. Meanwhile Dmitri had said outright, the day before, that he was glad Ivan was his rival, that it was a great help to him. How did it help him? To marry Grushenka? But Alyosha considered that the worst thing possible. Besides all this, right up until the evening before, Alyosha had firmly believed that Katerina Ivanovna held a steadfast, passionate love for Dmitri—but he had believed it only until the evening before. He had also imagined she was incapable of loving a man like Ivan, that she truly loved Dmitri, loved him exactly as he was, despite how strange such a passion was.

But during yesterday's scene with Grushenka, another thought had struck him. The word "lacerating," which Madame Khokhlakov had just used, nearly made him jump, because half-waking near daybreak that morning he had cried out "Laceration, laceration," probably applying it to something in his dream. He'd been dreaming all night about the previous day's scene at Katerina Ivanovna's. Now Alyosha found himself struck by Madame Khokhlakov's blunt, persistent claim that Katerina Ivanovna was in love with Ivan, and only deceived herself through some kind of pose, out of "self-laceration," tormenting herself with a pretended love for Dmitri out of some imagined duty of gratitude. "Yes," he thought, "maybe the whole truth is in those words." But then what was Ivan's position? Alyosha sensed instinctively that a character like Katerina Ivanovna's needed to dominate, and she could only dominate someone like Dmitri, never a man like Ivan. Dmitri, after all, might eventually submit to her rule "to his own happiness" (which was what Alyosha would have wished for), but Ivan—no, Ivan couldn't submit to her, and such submission wouldn't bring him happiness. Alyosha couldn't help believing that about Ivan. And now all these doubts and reflections flickered through his mind as he entered the drawing room. Another thought forced itself on him too: "What if she loved neither of them—neither Ivan nor Dmitri?"

It should be noted that Alyosha felt somewhat ashamed of his own thoughts and blamed himself whenever they kept recurring over the past month. "What do I know about love and women, and how can I judge such questions?" he thought reproachfully after such doubts and guesses. And yet it was impossible not to think about it. He sensed instinctively that this rivalry mattered enormously in his brothers' lives, and that a great deal hinged on it.

"One reptile will devour the other," Ivan had declared the day before, speaking in anger of his father and Dmitri. So Ivan regarded Dmitri as a reptile, and perhaps had for a long time. Was it, perhaps, ever since he'd known Katerina Ivanovna? That phrase had, of course, slipped out of Ivan unintentionally yesterday, but that only made it more significant. If he felt that way, what chance was there of peace? Weren't there, on the contrary, fresh grounds for hatred and hostility within the family? And which of them was Alyosha supposed to sympathize with? And what was he supposed to wish for each of them? He loved them both, but what could he wish for either one amid these conflicting interests? He might go completely astray in this maze, and Alyosha's heart couldn't bear uncertainty, because his love was always of an active kind. He was incapable of passive love. If he loved someone, he set to work at once to help them. And to do that he had to know what he was aiming at; he had to know for certain what was best for each one, and having determined that, it was natural for him to want to help them both. But instead of a clear goal, he found nothing but uncertainty and confusion on every side. "It was lacerating," as had just been said. But what could he even understand of this "laceration"? He didn't understand the first word of this bewildering maze.

Seeing Alyosha, Katerina Ivanovna said quickly and happily to Ivan, who had already gotten up to leave, "One minute! Stay just one more minute! I want to hear the opinion of this person here, whom I trust completely. Don't go," she added, turning to Madame Khokhlakov. She made Alyosha sit down beside her, and Madame Khokhlakov sat across from them, next to Ivan.

"You're all my friends here, all I have in the world, my dear friends," she began warmly, her voice trembling with genuine tears of suffering, and Alyosha's heart warmed to her at once. "You, Alexey Fyodorovitch, witnessed that appalling scene yesterday, and saw what I did. You didn't see it, Ivan Fyodorovitch—he did. What he thought of me yesterday, I don't know. I only know one thing: that if it happened again today, this very minute, I'd express the same feelings as yesterday—the same feelings, the same words, the same actions. You remember my actions, Alexey Fyodorovitch—you stopped me from one of them"—as she said this, she flushed and her eyes shone—"I have to tell you, I can't get past it. Listen, Alexey Fyodorovitch. I don't even know whether I still love him. I feel pity for him, and that's a poor sign of love. If I loved him, if I still loved him, maybe I wouldn't pity him now—I'd hate him."
Her voice trembled, and tears glittered on her eyelashes. Alyosha shuddered inwardly. "That girl is honest and sincere," he thought, "and she no longer loves Dmitri."
"That's true, that's true," cried Madame Khokhlakov.

"Wait, dear. I haven't told you the main thing, the final decision I reached during the night. I feel that this decision may be a terrible one—for me—but I can see that nothing will ever make me change it—nothing. It will be this way for the rest of my life. My dear, kind, ever-faithful and generous adviser, the one friend I have in the world, Ivan Fyodorovitch, with his deep insight into the heart, approves of and endorses my decision. He knows what it is."
"Yes, I approve of it," Ivan agreed, in a subdued but firm voice.

"But I'd also like Alyosha—ah, Alexey Fyodorovitch, forgive me for calling you simply Alyosha—I'd like Alexey Fyodorovitch, too, to tell me, in front of my two friends, whether I'm right. I sense instinctively that you, Alyosha, my dear brother—for you are a dear brother to me," she said again, ecstatically, taking his cold hand in her hot one, "I sense that your decision, your approval, will bring me peace despite all my suffering, because after your words I'll be calm and I'll submit—I feel that."

"I don't know what you're asking me," said Alyosha, flushing. "I only know that I love you, and right now I want your happiness more than my own!... But I know nothing about such matters," something drove him to add hastily.

"In such matters, Alexey Fyodorovitch, in such matters, the main thing is honor and duty and something higher—I don't know what—but higher, perhaps, even than duty. I'm aware of this irresistible feeling in my heart, and it compels me irresistibly. But it can all be put in two words. I've already decided—even if he marries that—creature," she began solemnly, "whom I can never, never forgive—even then I will not abandon him. From now on I will never, never abandon him!" she cried, breaking into a sort of pale, hysterical rapture. "Not that I'll chase after him constantly, get in his way, wear him down. Oh, no! I'll move away to another town—wherever you like—but I'll watch over him for the rest of my life—I'll watch over him ceaselessly, all my life. When he grows unhappy with that woman—and that's bound to happen very soon—let him come to me, and he'll find a friend, a sister.... Only a sister, of course, and forever; but he'll learn, at least, that this sister really is his sister, one who loves him and has sacrificed her whole life for him. I will win this. I will insist that he know me and confide in me completely, without reserve," she cried, in a kind of frenzy. "I will be a god he can pray to—and he owes me that much, at least, for his betrayal and for what I suffered through him yesterday. And let him see that for the rest of my life I will stay true to him and to the promise I gave him, no matter how unfaithful he is, no matter how he betrays me. I will—I will become nothing but a means to his happiness, or—how should I put it?—an instrument, a machine for his happiness, and that for my whole life, my whole life, so that he may see it for the rest of his! That's my decision. Ivan Fyodorovitch fully approves of it."

She was out of breath. She had perhaps meant to express her idea with more dignity, artistry, and naturalness, but her speech came out too rushed and raw. It was full of youthful impulsiveness, and it betrayed that she was still smarting from yesterday's insult, that her pride craved satisfaction. She felt this herself. Her face suddenly darkened, and an unpleasant look crossed her eyes. Alyosha noticed it at once and felt a pang of sympathy. His brother Ivan made it worse by adding:

"I've only expressed my own view," he said. "From anyone else, this would have sounded affected and overwrought. But from you—no. Any other woman would have been wrong, but you're right. I don't know how to explain it, but I can see that you're absolutely genuine, and that's why you're right."

"But that's only for the moment. And what does this moment amount to? Nothing but yesterday's insult." Madame Khokhlakov evidently hadn't intended to interrupt, but she couldn't hold back this perfectly fair comment.

"Just so, just so," Ivan cried, with unusual eagerness, clearly annoyed at being interrupted, "in anyone else this moment would only stem from yesterday's impression and would be just a moment. But with Katerina Ivanovna's character, that moment will last her whole life. What for anyone else would be only a promise is, for her, an everlasting, burdensome—grim, perhaps—but unwavering duty. And she'll be sustained by the sense of fulfilling that duty. Your life, Katerina Ivanovna, will from now on be spent in painful brooding over your own feelings, your own heroism, your own suffering; but in the end that suffering will soften and turn into sweet contemplation of the fulfillment of a bold, proud design. Yes, proud it certainly is, and desperate in any case, but a triumph for you all the same. And the awareness of it will, in the end, be a source of complete satisfaction and will reconcile you to everything else."
This was unmistakably said with a certain malice, and clearly on purpose—perhaps even with no real desire to hide that he was speaking ironically and deliberately.
"Oh, dear, how mistaken this all is!" Madame Khokhlakov cried again.
"Alexey Fyodorovitch, speak up. I desperately want to know what you'll say!" cried Katerina Ivanovna, and burst into tears. Alyosha got up from the sofa.

"It's nothing, nothing!" she went on through her tears. "I'm upset, I didn't sleep last night. But beside two such friends as you and your brother, I still feel strong—because I know you two will never desert me."
"Unfortunately I have to go back to Moscow—maybe tomorrow—and leave you for a long time. And unfortunately it can't be avoided," Ivan said suddenly.

"Tomorrow—to Moscow!" Her face contorted for an instant. "But—but, my goodness, how fortunate!" she cried, her voice suddenly changed. In an instant there was no trace of tears left. She underwent an instantaneous transformation that astonished Alyosha. Instead of a poor, wounded girl weeping in a fit of "laceration," he now saw a woman fully composed and even remarkably pleased, as if something delightful had just happened.

"Oh, not fortunate that I'm losing you, of course not," she corrected herself at once, with a charming, society smile. "A friend like you couldn't imagine I meant that. I'm only too unhappy to be losing you." She rushed impulsively at Ivan and, seizing both his hands, pressed them warmly. "But what's fortunate is that you'll be able, in Moscow, to see auntie and Agafya, and tell them the whole horror of my present situation. You can speak to Agafya with complete frankness, but spare dear auntie. You'll know how to manage that. You can't imagine how wretched I was, yesterday and this morning, trying to figure out how I could write them that dreadful letter—because some things simply can't be said in a letter.... Now it will be easy for me to write, because you'll see them and explain everything. Oh, how glad I am! But that's all I'm glad of, believe me. Of course, no one can take your place.... I'll go write the letter this instant," she finished suddenly, taking a step as if to leave the room.
"And what about Alyosha, and his opinion, which you were so desperate to hear?" cried Madame Khokhlakov. There was a sarcastic, angry note in her voice.

"I hadn't forgotten that," Katerina Ivanovna cried, stopping short. "And why are you being so hostile at a moment like this?" she added, with warm, bitter reproach. "What I said, I repeat. I must have his opinion. More than that, I must have his decision! Whatever he says, so it shall be. You see how anxious I am for your words, Alexey Fyodorovitch.... But what's wrong?"
"I couldn't have believed it. I can't understand it!" Alyosha cried suddenly, distressed.
"What? What?"

"He's going to Moscow, and you cry out that you're glad. You said that on purpose! And then you start explaining that you're not glad of that, but sorry to be losing a friend. But that was acting too—you were playing a part—like in a theater!"
"In a theater? What? What do you mean?" exclaimed Katerina Ivanovna, deeply astonished, flushing crimson, and frowning.

"Even while you're assuring him you're sorry to lose a friend in him, you keep telling him to his face that it's fortunate he's leaving," said Alyosha, breathlessly. He was standing at the table and hadn't sat down.
"What are you talking about? I don't understand."

"I don't understand it myself.... I seemed to see it all in a flash... I know I'm not saying it right, but I'll say it anyway," Alyosha went on in the same shaking, broken voice. "What I see is that maybe you don't love Dmitri at all... and never have, from the very beginning.... And Dmitri, too, has never loved you... he only respects you.... I really don't know how I dare say all this, but someone has to tell the truth... because no one here is telling the truth."
"What truth?" cried Katerina Ivanovna, and there was a hysterical edge to her voice.

"I'll tell you," Alyosha went on, with a kind of desperate haste, as if he were jumping off the roof of a house. "Send for Dmitri; I'll fetch him myself—let him come here, take your hand and take Ivan's, and join them together. Because you're torturing Ivan, simply because you love him—and you're torturing him because you love Dmitri through 'self-laceration'—with a false love—because you've talked yourself into it."
Alyosha broke off and fell silent.
"You... you... you're a little religious idiot—that's what you are!" Katerina Ivanovna snapped. Her face was white and her lips moved with anger.
Ivan suddenly laughed and got up. His hat was in his hand.

"You're mistaken, my good Alyosha," he said, with an expression Alyosha had never seen on his face before—an expression of youthful sincerity and strong, irresistibly frank feeling. "Katerina Ivanovna has never cared for me! She's known all along that I cared for her—though I never said a word of my love to her—she knew, but she didn't care for me. I've never even been her friend, not for a single moment; she's too proud to need my friendship. She kept me at her side as a means of revenge. Through me, and on me, she avenged all the insults she's continually received from Dmitri ever since they first met. Because even that first meeting has festered in her heart as an insult—that's the kind of heart she has! She's talked to me of nothing but her love for him. I'm leaving now; but believe me, Katerina Ivanovna, you really do love him. And the more he insults you, the more you love him—that's your 'laceration.' You love him exactly as he is; you love him for insulting you. If he reformed, you'd drop him at once and stop loving him. But you need him so you can go on contemplating your own heroic loyalty and reproaching him for his unfaithfulness. And it all comes from your pride. Oh, there's a great deal of humiliation and self-abasement mixed into it, but it all comes from pride.... I'm too young, and I've loved you too much. I know I shouldn't be saying this, that it would be more dignified of me simply to leave you, and less painful for you. But I'm going far away, and I'll never come back.... It's forever. I don't want to sit beside a 'laceration.'... But I don't know how to say it now. I've said everything.... Goodbye, Katerina Ivanovna, you can't be angry with me, because I'm punished a hundred times more severely than you, if only by the fact that I'll never see you again. Goodbye! I don't want your hand. You've tortured me too deliberately for me to be able to forgive you right now. I'll forgive you later, but right now I don't want your hand. 'Den Dank, Dame, begehr ich nicht,'" he added, with a forced smile, showing, all the same, that he could read Schiller, and had read him until he knew him by heart—something Alyosha would never have believed. He left the room without even saying goodbye to his hostess, Madame Khokhlakov. Alyosha clasped his hands together.

"Ivan!" he cried desperately after him. "Come back, Ivan! No, nothing will make him come back now!" he cried again, realizing it with regret. "But it's my fault, my fault. I started it! Ivan spoke angrily, wrongly. Unjustly and angrily. He has to come back here, come back," Alyosha kept exclaiming frantically.
Katerina Ivanovna suddenly went into the next room.
"You haven't done any harm. You behaved beautifully, like an angel," Madame Khokhlakov whispered rapidly, rapturously, to Alyosha. "I'll do everything I can to stop Ivan Fyodorovitch from leaving."
Her face glowed with delight, much to Alyosha's distress, but Katerina Ivanovna suddenly came back. She had two hundred-ruble notes in her hand.

"I have a great favor to ask of you, Alexey Fyodorovitch," she began, addressing him in a voice that sounded calm, even, as though nothing had happened. "A week ago—yes, I think it was a week ago—Dmitri Fyodorovitch committed a rash, unjust act—a very ugly act. There's a low tavern here, and in it he ran into that discharged officer, that captain your father used to employ for certain business. Dmitri Fyodorovitch, for some reason, lost his temper with this captain, grabbed him by the beard, and dragged him out into the street and some distance along it, in that humiliating way. And I'm told that his son, a boy, still a child, who goes to school here, saw it, and ran alongside them crying and begging for his father, appealing to everyone to defend him, while everyone laughed. You must forgive me, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I can't think without outrage of that disgraceful act of his... one of those acts only Dmitri Fyodorovitch is capable of, in his anger... and in his passions! I can't even describe it.... I can't find the words. I've made inquiries about his victim, and I find he's quite a poor man. His name is Snegiryov. He did something wrong in the army and was discharged. I don't know what, exactly. And now he's sunk into terrible poverty, with his family—an unhappy family of sick children, and, I believe, an insane wife. He's been living here a long time; he used to work as a copying clerk, but now he's getting nothing. I thought, if you... that is, I thought... I don't know. I'm so flustered. You see, I wanted to ask you, my dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, to go to him, to find some excuse to visit them—I mean the captain—oh, goodness, how badly I'm explaining this!—and delicately, carefully, the way only you know how," (Alyosha blushed), "manage to give him this assistance, these two hundred rubles. He'll be sure to take it.... I mean, persuade him to take it.... Or, rather, what do I mean? You see, it's not meant as compensation, to keep him from taking legal action, because I believe he meant to—but simply as a token of sympathy, a wish to help him, from me, Dmitri Fyodorovitch's betrothed, not from Dmitri himself.... But you understand.... I would go myself, but you'll know how to do it far better than I would. He lives on Lake Street, in the house of a woman named Kalmikov.... For God's sake, Alexey Fyodorovitch, do this for me, and now... now I'm rather... tired. Goodbye!"

She turned and vanished behind the curtain so quickly that Alyosha didn't have time to say a word, though he wanted to speak. He longed to ask her forgiveness, to blame himself, to say something, because his heart was full and he couldn't bear to leave the room without it. But Madame Khokhlakov took him by the hand and drew him along with her. In the hall she stopped him again, just as before.

"She's proud, she's struggling with herself, but kind, charming, generous," she exclaimed, in a half-whisper. "Oh, how I love her, especially at times like this, and how glad I am about everything all over again! Dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, you didn't know it, but I have to tell you: all of us—both her aunts, myself, all of us, even Lise—have spent the last month hoping and praying for nothing but that she'll give up your beloved Dmitri, who doesn't notice her and doesn't care for her, and marry Ivan Fyodorovitch instead—such an excellent, cultivated young man, who loves her more than anything in the world. We're all in on a regular conspiracy to bring it about, and that's possibly even part of why I'm still staying here."
"But she was crying—she's been hurt again," Alyosha cried.
"Never trust a woman's tears, Alexey Fyodorovitch. I'm never on the women's side in cases like this. I'm always on the men's side."
"Mamma, you're spoiling him," Lise's small voice called from behind the door.
"No, it was all my fault. I'm horribly to blame," Alyosha repeated, inconsolable, burying his face in his hands in an agony of remorse over his own thoughtlessness.
"Quite the opposite—you behaved like an angel, like an angel. I'm ready to say so a thousand times over."
"Mamma, how did he behave like an angel?" Lise's voice came again.
"For some reason I suddenly imagined," Alyosha went on, as though he hadn't heard Lise, "that she loved Ivan, and that's why I said that stupid thing.... What's going to happen now?"
"Loved who, loved who?" cried Lise. "Mamma, you really want to be the death of me. I ask you and you don't answer."
Just then the maid ran in.
"Katerina Ivanovna is ill.... She's crying, struggling... hysterics."
"What's wrong?" cried Lise, in a tone of real alarm. "Mamma, I'm going to have hysterics, not her!"

"Lise, for mercy's sake, don't scream, don't torment me. At your age one can't know everything that grown-up people know. I'll come and tell you everything you ought to know. Oh, mercy on us! I'm coming, I'm coming.... Hysterics is a good sign, Alexey Fyodorovitch, it's excellent that she's hysterical. That's exactly as it should be. In cases like this I'm always against the woman, against all this feminine crying and hysterics. Run and tell her, Yulia, that I'll fly to her. As for Ivan Fyodorovitch leaving like that, it's her own doing. But he won't leave. Lise, for mercy's sake, don't scream! Oh, yes, you're not screaming, it's me who's screaming. Forgive your mamma, but I'm delighted, delighted, delighted! Did you notice, Alexey Fyodorovitch, how young, how young Ivan Fyodorovitch looked just now, leaving like that, saying all that and walking out? I'd thought he was so learned, such a scholar, and all of a sudden he behaved so warmly, so openly, so youthfully, with such youthful inexperience, and it was all so fine, so like you.... And the way he recited that German verse, that was just like you too! But I must fly, I must fly! Alexey Fyodorovitch, hurry and carry out her errand, then hurry back.
