Lise, do you need anything right now? For mercy's sake, don't keep Alexey Fyodorovitch even a minute. He'll come right back to you."
Madame Khokhlakov finally ran off. Before leaving, Alyosha would have opened the door to see Lise.
"Absolutely not," Lise cried. "Not now, on any account. Talk through the door. How did you come to be an angel? That's the only thing I want to know."
"For a terrible piece of stupidity, Lise! Goodbye!"
"Don't you dare walk away like that!" Lise began.
"Lise, I have a real sorrow! I'll be back soon, but I have a great, great sorrow!"
And he ran out of the room.

title: VI. A Laceration In The Cottage
paragraphs: He truly was grieved, in a way he'd rarely been before. He'd charged in like a fool and meddled in what? A love affair. "But what do I know about it? What can I possibly say about such things?" he repeated to himself for the hundredth time, blushing crimson. "Oh, being embarrassed would be nothing—embarrassment is just the punishment I deserve. The real trouble is that I've almost certainly caused more unhappiness.... And Father Zosima sent me to reconcile them, to bring them together. Is this the way to bring them together?" Then he suddenly remembered how he'd tried to join their hands, and felt a fresh wave of shame. "Even though I acted sincerely, I need to be more sensible going forward," he concluded suddenly, and didn't even smile at the thought.

Katerina Ivanovna's errand took him to Lake Street, and his brother Dmitri lived nearby, just off Lake Street. Alyosha decided to look in on him before going to the captain, though he had a feeling he wouldn't find his brother home. He suspected Dmitri would be deliberately avoiding him now, but he had to find him regardless. Time was slipping by: the thought of his dying elder hadn't left Alyosha for a single minute since he'd set out from the monastery.

One point about Katerina Ivanovna's errand interested him in particular. When she'd mentioned the captain's son, the little schoolboy who had run alongside his father crying, the thought had struck Alyosha at once that this must be the same schoolboy who had bitten his finger when he'd asked what he'd done to hurt him. Now Alyosha felt almost certain of it, though he couldn't have said why. It was a relief to think about something else, and he resolved not to dwell any further on the "mischief" he'd caused, not to torment himself with remorse, but simply to do what needed doing, come what may. That thought settled him completely. Turning onto the street where Dmitri lodged, he felt hungry, and taking the roll he'd brought from his father's out of his pocket, he ate it. It made him feel stronger.

Dmitri wasn't home. The people of the house—an old cabinetmaker, his son, and his old wife—eyed Alyosha with outright suspicion. "He hasn't slept here the last three nights. Maybe he's gone away," the old man said in answer to Alyosha's persistent questions. Alyosha could tell he was answering as instructed. When he asked whether Dmitri might be at Grushenka's, or hiding out at Foma's (Alyosha spoke this freely on purpose), all three looked at him with alarm. "They're fond of him, they're doing their best for him," thought Alyosha. "That's good."

At last he found the house on Lake Street. It was a decrepit little house, sunk on one side, with three windows facing the street and a muddy yard where a single cow stood. He crossed the yard and found the door leading into the passage. On the left of the passage lived the old woman who owned the house, along with her elderly daughter. Both seemed to be deaf. In answer to his repeated questions about the captain, one of them finally understood he was asking after their tenants, and pointed to a door across the passage. The captain's lodging turned out to be a plain cottage room. Alyosha had his hand on the iron latch when he was struck by the strange hush inside. Yet he knew from Katerina Ivanovna's account that the man had a family. "Either they're all asleep, or maybe they heard me coming and are waiting for me to open the door. I'd better knock first," and he knocked. An answer came, but not right away—after a pause of maybe ten seconds.
"Who's there?" someone shouted in a loud, very angry voice.

Then Alyosha opened the door and stepped over the threshold. He found himself in a proper peasant room. Though it was large, it was cluttered with all kinds of household belongings, and there were several people in it. On the left stood a big Russian stove. A string ran from the stove across the room to the window on the left, with rags hanging from it. There was a bedstead against the wall on each side, left and right, covered with knitted quilts. On the one to the left sat a pyramid of four print-covered pillows, each smaller than the one beneath. On the other there was only one very small pillow. The opposite corner was screened off by a curtain, or a sheet hung on a string. Behind this curtain a bed made up on a bench and a chair was visible. A rough, plain wooden table had been pushed up to the middle window. The three windows, each made of four tiny, greenish, mildewed panes, let in little light, and were shut tight, so the room was dim and rather stuffy. On the table stood a frying pan with the remains of some fried eggs, a half-eaten piece of bread, and a small bottle with a few drops of vodka left in it.

A genteel-looking woman in a cotton dress sat on a chair by the bed on the left. Her face was thin and sallow, and her sunken cheeks made it obvious at a glance that she was ill. But what struck Alyosha most was the look in the poor woman's eyes—a mixture of startled inquiry and haughty pride. While he talked with her husband, her large brown eyes moved from one speaker to the other with that same haughty, questioning look. Beside her at the window stood a young girl, rather plain, with thin reddish hair, poorly but very neatly dressed. She looked at Alyosha with disdain as he came in. Beside the other bed sat another female figure. She was a very sad sight—a young woman of about twenty, but hunchbacked and crippled, "with withered legs," as Alyosha learned afterward. Her crutches stood in the corner nearby. This poor girl's strikingly beautiful, gentle eyes gazed at Alyosha with mild serenity. A man of forty-five sat at the table, finishing the fried eggs. He was thin, small, weakly built. He had reddish hair and a sparse, light-colored beard that closely resembled a wisp of tow—this comparison, and the phrase "wisp of tow," flashed into Alyosha's mind at once for some reason; he remembered it afterward. It was clearly this man who had shouted at him, since there was no other man in the room. But the moment Alyosha stepped in, he leapt up from the bench he'd been sitting on, and hastily wiping his mouth with a ragged napkin, darted over to Alyosha.

"It's a monk come begging for the monastery. A fine place to come to!" the girl standing in the left corner said aloud. The man spun around toward her instantly and answered in an excited, cracking voice:
"No, Varvara, you're wrong. Allow me to ask," he turned back to Alyosha, "what has brought you to—our little retreat?"

Alyosha looked at him closely. This was the first time he'd seen him. There was something angular, flustered, and irritable about him. Though he'd clearly just been drinking, he wasn't drunk. His expression showed an extraordinary insolence, and yet, oddly, at the same time a kind of fear. He looked like a man who'd been kept under someone's thumb for a long time and had submitted to it, but had now suddenly turned and was trying to assert himself. Or, better yet, like a man who desperately wants to hit you but is terrified you'll hit him back. In his words, and in the pitch of his shrill voice, there was a sort of manic humor, sometimes spiteful, sometimes cringing, shifting constantly from one tone to another. He'd asked the question about "our little retreat" practically trembling all over, rolling his eyes, and hopping up so close to Alyosha that Alyosha instinctively stepped back. He wore a very shabby dark cotton coat, patched and stained. His checked trousers were an extremely light color, long out of fashion, made of very thin material. They were so wrinkled and short that he looked like he'd outgrown them like a boy.
"I'm Alexey Karamazov," Alyosha began, by way of answer.
"I understand that perfectly well, sir," the man snapped out at once, to prove he already knew who he was. "I'm Captain Snegiryov, sir, but I'm still eager to know exactly what's led you—"
"Oh, I've come for nothing in particular. I wanted a word with you—if you'll allow it."

"In that case, here's a chair, sir; kindly be seated. That's what they used to say in the old comedies, 'kindly be seated,'" and with a quick gesture he grabbed an empty chair—a rough wooden one, not upholstered—and set it down almost in the middle of the room; then, taking another chair like it for himself, he sat down facing Alyosha, so close their knees nearly touched.

"Nikolay Ilyitch Snegiryov, sir, formerly a captain in the Russian infantry, disgraced for his vices, but a captain all the same. Though I might not sound much like one anymore, given how I talk—for the last half of my life I've learned to say 'sir.' It's a word you pick up once you've come down in the world."
"That's very true," Alyosha smiled. "But do you say it without meaning to, or on purpose?"

"As God's my witness, it's involuntary—I never used it before! I never said 'sir' in my life, but the moment I sank into hard times I started saying it. It's the work of some higher power. I see you're interested in matters of the day, but how could I possibly have caught your curiosity, living the way I do, in surroundings where hospitality is out of the question?"
"I've come—about that business."
"What business?" the captain broke in impatiently.
"About your run-in with my brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch," Alyosha blurted out awkwardly.

"What run-in, sir? You don't mean that one? About my 'wisp of tow,' then?" He leaned in closer, so that his knees actually knocked against Alyosha's. His lips had pressed together strangely, like a thread.
"What wisp of tow?" Alyosha murmured.

"He's come to complain about me, father!" cried a voice Alyosha recognized—the schoolboy's voice—from behind the curtain. "I bit his finger just now." The curtain was pulled back, and Alyosha saw his attacker lying on a small bed made up on the bench and chair in the corner beneath the icons. The boy lay covered with his coat and an old quilted blanket. He was clearly unwell, and judging by his glittering eyes, feverish. He looked at Alyosha without fear, as though he felt safe at home and beyond reach.
"What! He bit your finger?" The captain jumped up from his chair. "It was your finger he bit?"

"Yes. He was throwing stones with the other schoolboys. There were six of them against him, alone. I went over to him, and he threw a stone at me, then another one at my head. I asked him what I'd done to him. And then he flew at me and bit my finger badly—I don't know why."
"I'll thrash him, sir, right now—this instant!" The captain sprang up from his seat.
"But I'm not complaining at all, I'm just telling you... I don't want him thrashed. Besides, he seems to be ill."

"And do you suppose I'd actually thrash him? That I'd take my Ilyusha and beat him in front of you, just to satisfy you? Would you like it done right now, sir?" the captain said, suddenly turning on Alyosha as though about to attack him. "I'm sorry about your finger, sir; but instead of thrashing Ilyusha, would you like me to chop off four of my own fingers with this knife here, in front of your eyes, to satisfy your righteous anger? I should think four fingers would be enough to satisfy your thirst for revenge. You won't ask for the fifth one too, will you?" He stopped short, his throat catching. Every feature in his face twitched and worked; he looked fiercely defiant. He was in a kind of frenzy.

"I think I understand it all now," Alyosha said gently, sorrowfully, still sitting where he was. "So your boy is a good boy, he loves his father, and he attacked me as the brother of the man who attacked you.... Now I understand," he repeated thoughtfully. "But my brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch regrets what he did, I know that for certain, and if it's at all possible for him to come here, or better, to meet you in that same place, he'll ask your forgiveness in front of everyone—if that's what you want."
"After yanking out my beard, you mean, he'll ask my forgiveness? And he thinks that'll settle things nicely, does he?"
"Oh, no! On the contrary, he'll do anything you like, in any way you like."
"So if I asked his lordship to go down on his knees in front of me, right there in that very tavern—'The Metropolis,' it's called—or in the marketplace, he'd do it?"
"Yes, he'd even go down on his knees."

"You've pierced me to the heart, sir. Touched me to tears, pierced me to the heart! I'm only too aware of your brother's generosity. Allow me to introduce my family—my two daughters, and my son—my little brood. If I die, who'll look after them, and while I live, who but they will care for a wretch like me? That's a great thing the Lord has arranged for every man of my sort, sir. Because there has to be someone able to love even a man like me."
"Ah, that's perfectly true!" Alyosha exclaimed.
"Oh, do stop playing the fool! Some idiot walks in and you make a spectacle of us!" cried the girl by the window, turning to her father suddenly with a disdainful, contemptuous air.
"Just wait, Varvara!" her father cried peremptorily, though he looked at her with obvious approval. "That's her character," he said, turning back to Alyosha.
"'And in all of nature there was nothing / That could find favor in his eyes—'

or rather, in the feminine—that could find favor in her eyes. But now let me introduce you to my wife, Arina Petrovna. She's crippled, she's forty-three; she can move, but only just barely. She comes from humble origins. Arina Petrovna, compose yourself. This is Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov. Stand up, Alexey Fyodorovitch." He took him by the hand and, with surprising force, pulled him to his feet. "You have to stand to be introduced to a lady. It's not the Karamazov, mamma, who... hm... et cetera, but his brother, shining with modest virtues. Come, Arina Petrovna, come, mamma, your hand first, to be kissed."

And he kissed his wife's hand respectfully, even tenderly. The girl at the window turned her back on the whole scene, indignant; an expression of extraordinary warmth came over the haughtily questioning face of the woman.
"Good morning! Sit down, Mr. Tchernomazov," she said.
"Karamazov, mamma, Karamazov. We come from humble origins," he whispered again.

"Well, Karamazov, or whatever it is, but I always think of it as Tchernomazov.... Sit down. Why did he yank you up like that? He calls me crippled, but I'm not, it's just that my legs are swollen up like barrels, while the rest of me has shriveled away. I used to be quite plump once, but now it's as if I'd swallowed a needle."
"We come from humble origins," the captain muttered again.
"Oh, father, father!" the hunchbacked girl, who had been silent in her chair until now, suddenly said, burying her eyes in her handkerchief.
"Buffoon!" the girl at the window blurted out.

"Have you heard our news?" the mother said, gesturing at her daughters. "It's like clouds rolling in; the clouds pass and we have music again. When we lived with the regiment, we used to have plenty of guests like this. I'm not trying to make comparisons, mind you—each to his own taste. The deacon's wife used to come by back then and say, 'Alexandr Alexandrovitch has the noblest heart there is, but Nastasya Petrovna,' she'd say, 'comes straight out of hell.' 'Well,' I told her, 'that's a matter of taste, but you're a little spitfire yourself.' 'And you need putting in your place,' says she. 'You black-tongued thing,' said I, 'who asked you to lecture me?' 'But my breath,' says she, 'is clean, and yours isn't.' 'Go ask any of the officers whether my breath is unclean.' And ever since, it's stuck in my mind. Not long ago I was sitting right here, just as I am now, when that very general walked in, the one who came for Easter, and I asked him: 'Your Excellency,' I said, 'can a lady's breath be unpleasant?' 'Yes,' he answered, 'you ought to crack a windowpane or open the door, the air in here isn't fresh.' And they all go on like that! And what's my breath to them, anyway? The dead smell far worse! 'I won't spoil the air,' I told them, 'I'll order some slippers and be on my way.' My darlings, don't blame your own mother! Nikolay Ilyitch, how is it I can never please you? Only Ilyusha, when he comes home from school, loves me. Yesterday he brought me an apple. Forgive your own mother—forgive a poor, lonely creature! Why has my breath grown so unpleasant to you?"
And the poor, deranged woman burst into sobs, tears streaming down her cheeks. The captain rushed to her side.

"Mamma, mamma, my dear, stop! You're not lonely. Everyone loves you, everyone adores you." He began kissing both her hands again and tenderly stroking her face; taking the dinner napkin, he wiped away her tears. Alyosha thought he saw tears in the captain's own eyes too. "There, you see, you hear?" he turned toward Alyosha with a kind of fury, pointing at the poor, addled woman.
"I see and I hear," Alyosha murmured.
"Father, father, how could you—with him! Leave him be!" the boy cried, sitting up in bed and staring at his father with burning eyes.
"Would you stop clowning around, putting on your silly performances that never lead anywhere!" Varvara shouted, stamping her foot in a rage.

"Your anger is entirely fair this time, Varvara, and I'll hurry to satisfy you. Come, put on your cap, Alexey Fyodorovitch, and I'll put on mine. Let's go outside. I have something serious to say to you, but not within these walls. This girl sitting here is my daughter Nina; I forgot to introduce her. She's a heavenly angel come to earth... flown down to us mortals... if you can understand what I mean."
"There he is, shaking all over, as if he's having a fit!" Varvara went on indignantly.

"And that one there, stamping her foot at me and calling me a fool just now, she's a heavenly angel come to earth too, and she has every right to call me that. Come along, Alexey Fyodorovitch, we need to finish this."
And, grabbing Alyosha's hand, he pulled him out of the room and into the street.

title: VII. And In The Open Air
paragraphs: "The air is fresh, but in my apartment it isn't, not in any sense of the word. Let's walk slowly, sir. I'd be glad of your kind attention."
"I have something important to tell you too," Alyosha remarked, "only I don't know how to begin."

"Of course you must have business with me. You'd never have come to see me without some reason. Unless you've come simply to complain about the boy, which seems unlikely. And speaking of the boy—I couldn't explain it to you back there, but I'll describe that scene to you now. My tow was thicker a week ago—I mean my beard. That's the nickname they've given my beard, the schoolboys especially. Well, your brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch was dragging me by my beard—I hadn't done a thing, he was in a towering rage and happened to run into me. He hauled me out of the tavern into the marketplace; just then the boys were coming out of school, and Ilyusha with them. The moment he saw me in that state, he ran up to me. 'Father,' he cried, 'father!' He grabbed hold of me, hugged me, tried to pull me away, crying to the man attacking me, 'Let go, let go, it's my father, forgive him!'—yes, he actually cried 'forgive him.' He clutched at that hand, that very hand, in his little hands and kissed it.... I remember his little face at that moment, I haven't forgotten it and I never will!"

"I swear," cried Alyosha, "that my brother will express his deepest, most sincere regret, even if he has to go down on his knees in that very marketplace.... I'll make him do it, or he's no brother of mine!"

"Ah, so it's only a suggestion! It doesn't come from him at all, just from the generosity of your own warm heart. You should have said so from the start. No—in that case, allow me to tell you about your brother's highly chivalrous, soldierly generosity, because he did display it at the time. He stopped dragging me by the beard and let me go: 'You're an officer,' he said, 'and I'm an officer—if you can find a decent man to act as your second, send me your challenge. I'll give you satisfaction, even though you're a scoundrel.' That's what he said. A chivalrous spirit indeed! I withdrew with Ilyusha, and that scene is a family memory now, printed on Ilyusha's soul forever. No, sir, it's not for us to claim the privileges of noblemen. Judge for yourself. You've just been in our mansion—what did you see there? Three ladies, one a cripple and feeble-minded, another a cripple and hunchbacked, and the third not crippled but far too clever for her own good. She's a student, desperate to get back to Petersburg, to work for the emancipation of the Russian woman on the banks of the Neva. I won't even mention Ilyusha, he's only nine. I'm alone in the world, and if I die, what becomes of all of them? I simply ask you that. And if I challenge him and he kills me on the spot, what then? What becomes of them? And worse still, if he doesn't kill me but only cripples me—I couldn't work, but I'd still be a mouth to feed. Who would feed that mouth, and who would feed all the rest of them? Must I pull Ilyusha out of school and send him to beg in the streets? That's what challenging him to a duel would mean for me. It's foolish talk and nothing more."
"He will beg your forgiveness, he'll bow down at your feet in the middle of the marketplace," Alyosha cried again, his eyes glowing.

"I did think about prosecuting him," the captain went on, "but look at our code—could I really get much compensation for a personal injury? And then Agrafena Alexandrovna sent for me and shouted at me: 'Don't you dare dream of it! If you take him to court, I'll announce to the whole world that he beat you for your dishonesty, and then it's you who'll be prosecuted.' I call God to witness whose dishonesty it actually was, and whose orders I was acting under—wasn't it hers and Fyodor Pavlovitch's? 'And what's more,' she went on, 'I'll dismiss you for good, and you'll never earn another penny from me. I'll speak to my merchant too'—that's what she calls her old man—'and he'll dismiss you as well!' And if he dismisses me, where else could I earn anything? Those two are all I have to rely on, because your Fyodor Pavlovitch has not only stopped employing me, for other reasons, but means to use some papers I've signed to take me to court himself. So I kept quiet, and now you've seen our little retreat. But let me ask you—did Ilyusha hurt your finger badly? I didn't want to go into it back there in our mansion, in front of him."

"Yes, quite badly, and he was in a real fury. He was avenging you on me, as a Karamazov, I understand that now. But if only you'd seen how he was throwing stones at his schoolmates! It's very dangerous. They could kill him. Children are foolish. A thrown stone can crack someone's skull open."
"That's exactly what happened. He got bruised by a stone today. Not on the head, on the chest, just above the heart. He came home crying and groaning, and now he's ill."
"And you know, he attacks them first. He's bitter at them on your account. They say he stabbed a boy named Krassotkin with a penknife not long ago."
"I've heard about that too, it's dangerous. Krassotkin is an official here, we may hear more about it yet."
"I'd advise you," Alyosha went on warmly, "not to send him to school at all for a while, until he's calmer... until his anger has passed."

"Anger!" the captain repeated. "That's exactly what it is. He's a small creature, but it's a mighty anger. You don't know the whole of it, sir. Let me tell you more. Ever since that incident, all the boys have been teasing him about the 'wisp of tow.' Schoolboys are a merciless breed—individually they're angels, but together, especially at school, they're often merciless. Their teasing has stirred up a gallant spirit in Ilyusha. An ordinary boy, a weak-willed son, would have caved, felt ashamed of his father, sir, but he stood up for his father against every one of them. For his father, and for truth and justice. Because what he went through when he kissed your brother's hand and cried out, 'Forgive father, forgive him'—only God knows that, and I do, his father. Our children—not your children, but ours, the children of poor gentlemen looked down on by everyone—know what justice means, sir, even at nine years old. How could rich children know it? They never plumb such depths, not once in their lives. But at that moment in the square, when he kissed that hand, at that moment my Ilyusha grasped the whole meaning of justice. That truth entered him and crushed him forever, sir," the captain said, heated again, in a kind of frenzy, striking his right fist against his left palm as if to show how "the truth" had crushed Ilyusha. "That very day, sir, he came down with a fever and was delirious all night. All that day he'd barely said a word to me, but I noticed he kept watching me out of the corner of his eye, even though he'd turned to the window and pretended to be studying his lessons. But I could see his mind wasn't on his lessons at all. The next day I got drunk to forget my troubles, sinful man that I am, and I don't remember much. Mamma started crying too—I'm very fond of mamma—well, I spent my last kopek drowning my sorrows. Don't think less of me for that, sir—in Russia the men who drink are often the best men. The best among us are the biggest drunkards. I lay down and don't remember what happened with Ilyusha, though the boys had been jeering at him at school all that day. 'Wisp of tow,' they shouted, 'your father was dragged out of the tavern by his wisp of tow, and you ran along behind begging forgiveness.'"

"On the third day, when he came home from school, I saw he looked pale and wretched. 'What is it?' I asked. He wouldn't answer. Well, there's no talking privately in our mansion without mamma and the girls joining in. What's more, the girls had heard about it the very first day. Varvara had started snarling. 'You fools, you buffoons, can't you ever do anything sensible?' 'Quite right,' I said, 'can we ever do anything sensible?' For the moment I brushed it off like that. So that evening I took the boy out for a walk, because you should know we go walking every evening, always the same route, the one we're walking now—from our gate to that big stone lying by itself in the road, under the fence, which marks the start of the town pasture. A beautiful, lonely spot, sir. Ilyusha and I walked along hand in hand, as usual. He has a small hand, his fingers thin and cold—his chest troubles him, you know. 'Father,' he said, 'father!' 'Yes?' I said. I saw his eyes flash. 'Father, the way he treated you!' 'It can't be helped, Ilyusha,' I said. 'Don't forgive him, father, don't forgive him! At school they say he paid you ten rubles for it.' 'No, Ilyusha,' I said, 'I wouldn't take money from him for anything.' Then he started trembling all over, took my hand in both of his, and kissed it again. 'Father,' he said, 'father, challenge him to a duel—at school they say you're a coward and won't challenge him, and that you'll take ten rubles from him.' 'I can't challenge him to a duel, Ilyusha,' I answered. And I explained briefly what I've just told you. He listened. 'Father,' he said, 'still, don't forgive it. When I grow up I'll challenge him myself and kill him.' His eyes were burning, blazing. And of course, being his father, I had to say something: 'It's a sin to kill,' I said, 'even in a duel.' 'Father,' he said, 'when I grow up, I'll knock him down, knock the sword right out of his hand, I'll throw myself on him, wave my sword over him, and say: "I could kill you, but I forgive you—so there!"' You can see what's been going on in that small mind of his these last two days; he must have been plotting that revenge all day and raving about it half the night.

"But then he started coming home from school badly beaten—I found out about it the day before yesterday—and you're right, I won't send him to that school anymore. I heard he'd been standing up against the whole class alone, defying every one of them, that his heart was full of resentment, of bitterness—it worried me. We went for another walk. 'Father,' he asked, 'are rich people stronger than everyone else on earth?' 'Yes, Ilyusha,' I said, 'there's no one on earth stronger than the rich.' 'Father,' he said, 'I'll get rich, I'll become an officer and beat everyone. The Tsar will reward me, I'll come back here, and then no one will dare—' Then he fell silent, his lips still trembling. 'Father,' he said, 'what a horrible town this is.' 'Yes, Ilyusha,' I said, 'it's not a very nice town.' 'Father, let's move to another town, a nice one,' he said, 'where people don't know about us.' 'We'll move, we will, Ilyusha,' I said, 'only I need to save up for it.' I was glad to be able to steer his mind away from painful thoughts, and we started dreaming about how we'd move to another town, how we'd buy a horse and cart. 'We'll put mamma and your sisters inside, tuck them in, and we'll walk—you can ride for a bit now and then, and I'll walk alongside, because we have to spare the horse, we can't all ride at once. That's how we'll go.' He was thrilled at that, especially at the thought of having a horse and driving it. Of course a Russian boy is born loving horses. We talked on like that for a long while. Thank God, I thought, I've managed to distract him and comfort him.

"That was the evening before yesterday, but last night everything changed. He'd gone to school in the morning, came home depressed, terribly depressed. In the evening I took him by the hand and we went for our walk; he wouldn't talk. The wind was blowing, no sun, that autumn feeling in the air; twilight was coming on. We walked along, both of us gloomy. 'Well, my boy,' I said, 'what about setting off on our travels?' I was hoping to bring him back to our talk from the day before. He didn't answer, but I felt his fingers trembling in my hand. Ah, I thought, this is bad; something's happened. We'd reached the stone where we're standing now. I sat down on it. And in the sky there were kites everywhere, flapping and wheeling. As many as thirty in sight. Of course, it's just the season for kites. 'Look, Ilyusha,' I said, 'it's time we got out last year's kite again. I'll mend it—where did you put it away?' My boy said nothing. He looked away, turned sideways from me. Then a gust of wind kicked up the sand. He suddenly fell against me, threw both his little arms around my neck, and held on tight. You know how children get, when they're silent and proud and try to hold back their tears through some great trouble, and then suddenly break down—their tears come in streams. With those warm streams of tears, he suddenly soaked my face. He sobbed and shook as if he were having a fit, pressing himself against me as I sat on the stone. 'Father,' he kept crying, 'dear father, how he insulted you!' And I sobbed too. We sat there shaking in each other's arms. 'Ilyusha,' I said to him, 'Ilyusha, darling.' No one saw us then. Only God saw us, and I hope He'll count it in my favor. You should thank your brother, Alexey Fyodorovitch. No, sir, I won't thrash my boy just to satisfy you."

He had slipped back into his original tone of resentful clowning. Alyosha sensed, though, that the man trusted him, and that if someone else had been standing in Alyosha's place, the captain wouldn't have spoken so openly, wouldn't have told him what he'd just told him. This encouraged Alyosha, whose heart was trembling on the edge of tears.
"Ah, how I'd like to be friends with your boy!" he exclaimed. "If you could arrange it—"
"Certainly, sir," the captain murmured.

"But now, listen to something else entirely!" Alyosha went on. "I have a message for you. That same brother of mine, Dmitri, has also insulted his fiancée, a noble-hearted young woman you've probably heard of. I have the right to tell you about the wrong done to her; in fact, I ought to, because when she heard about the insult done to you and learned about your unfortunate situation, she instructed me at once—just now—to bring you this help from her—only from her, not from Dmitri, who has abandoned her. Not from me, his brother, either, nor from anyone else—from her, only from her! She begs you to accept her help.... You've both been insulted by the same man. She thought of you the moment she'd received a similar insult from him—similar in its cruelty, I mean. She comes to you like a sister helping a brother in trouble.... She told me to convince you to take these two hundred rubles from her, as from a sister, knowing how badly you need it. No one will ever know, it can't give rise to any unjust gossip. Here are the two hundred rubles, and I swear you must take them—unless all men on earth are meant to be enemies! But there are brothers on this earth too.... You have a generous heart... you must see that, you must," and Alyosha held out two crisp, rainbow-colored hundred-ruble notes.

They were both standing by the big stone near the fence at that moment, and there was no one nearby. The notes seemed to hit the captain like a shock. He started, but at first only from sheer astonishment. Such an outcome to their conversation was the last thing he'd expected. Nothing could have been further from his mind than help from anyone—let alone a sum like that!
He took the notes, and for a moment could barely speak, an entirely new expression crossing his face.
"That's for me? So much money—two hundred rubles! Good heavens! Why, I haven't seen that much money in the last four years! Mercy on us! And she says she's a sister.... And that's really true?"
"I swear that everything I've told you is the truth," Alyosha cried.
The captain flushed red.

"Listen, my dear friend, listen. If I take it, won't I be behaving like a scoundrel? In your eyes, Alexey Fyodorovitch, won't I be a scoundrel? No, Alexey Fyodorovitch, listen, listen," he hurried on, touching Alyosha with both hands. "You're persuading me to take it, saying it comes from a sister, but deep down, in your heart, won't you feel contempt for me if I take it, eh?"
"No, no, I swear on my salvation I won't! And no one will ever know except me—me, you, her, and one other lady, her closest friend."

"Never mind the lady! Listen, Alexey Fyodorovitch, at a moment like this you need to listen, because you can't understand what these two hundred rubles mean to me right now." The poor man was working himself up, little by little, into a kind of incoherent, almost wild enthusiasm. He'd been knocked off balance and talked extremely fast, as if afraid he wouldn't be allowed to say everything he had to say.

"Besides the fact that it's honestly earned, coming from a 'sister' so deeply respected and revered—do you realize that now I can look after mamma and Nina, my hunchbacked angel of a daughter? Doctor Herzenstube came to see me, out of the kindness of his heart, and examined them both for a full hour. 'I can't make anything of it,' he said, but he prescribed a mineral water sold at a chemist's here. He said it would be sure to help her, and he ordered hot baths too, with some medicine dissolved in them. The mineral water costs thirty kopeks, and she'd need maybe forty bottles of it; so I took the prescription and laid it on the shelf under the icons, and there it's stayed. And he ordered hot baths for Nina, with something dissolved in them, morning and evening. But how can we manage a cure like that in our mansion, with no servants, no help, no bath, and no water? Nina has rheumatism all over, I don't think I mentioned that. Her whole right side aches at night, she's in agony, and would you believe it, the angel bears it without a groan, for fear of waking us. We eat whatever we can get, and she'll only take the leftovers, scraps you'd barely give a dog. 'I'm not worth it, I'm taking it from you, I'm a burden on you'—that's what her angel eyes seem to say. We wait on her, but she hates it. 'I'm a useless cripple, no good to anyone.' As if she weren't worth it, when she's the saving grace of all of us with her angelic sweetness. Without her, without her gentle voice, it would be hell in that house! She softens even Varvara. And don't judge Varvara too harshly either, she's an angel too, she's suffered wrong as well. She came to us for the summer, bringing sixteen rubles she'd earned and saved from giving lessons, meaning to go back to Petersburg with it in September—which is now. But we spent her money and lived on it, so now she has nothing to go back with. Though really she couldn't go back anyway, since she has to slave for us like a servant. She's like an overworked horse with all of us riding on her back. She waits on everyone, mends and washes, sweeps the floors, puts mamma to bed. And mamma is moody, and tearful, and out of her mind! And now, with this money, I can hire a servant, do you understand, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I can buy medicine for these dear creatures, I can send my student off to Petersburg, I can buy beef, feed them properly. Good Lord, it's like a dream!"
Alyosha was delighted that he'd brought the man such happiness, and that the poor fellow had let himself be made happy.

"Wait, Alexey Fyodorovitch, wait," the captain began, talking with a frenzied rush, swept up in a new daydream. "Do you know, Ilyusha and I might actually manage to carry out our dream after all. We'll buy a horse and cart, a black horse—he insists it has to be black—and we'll set off just as we imagined the other day. I have an old friend, a lawyer in K—— province, and I've heard from a reliable man that if I went to him, he'd give me a clerk's position in his office—so who knows, maybe he really would. I'd just put mamma and Nina in the cart, and Ilyusha could drive, and I'd walk, I'd walk alongside.... Why, if I could just manage to collect one debt that's owed me, I might have enough for that too!"

"There would be enough!" Alyosha cried. "Katerina Ivanovna will send you as much more as you need, and you know, I have money too, take whatever you need, as you would from a brother, a friend, you can pay it back later.... (You'll get rich, you'll get rich!) And you know, you couldn't have a better idea than moving to another province! It would be your salvation, especially your boy's—and you should go soon, before winter, before the cold sets in. You must write to us once you're there, and we'll always be like brothers.... No, it's not a dream!"

Alyosha could have hugged him, he was so pleased. But glancing at him, he stopped short. The man stood with his neck stretched out and his lips protruding, his face pale and frenzied. His lips were moving as though trying to form words; no sound came out, but still his lips moved. It was unsettling.
"What is it?" Alyosha asked, startled.

"Alexey Fyodorovitch... I... you," the captain muttered, stumbling over his words, staring at him with a strange, wild, fixed look, an air of desperate resolve. At the same time there was a sort of grin on his lips. "I... you, sir... wouldn't you like me to show you a little trick I know?" he murmured suddenly, in a firm, quick whisper, his voice no longer faltering.
"What trick?"
"A pretty trick," the captain whispered. His mouth twisted at the left corner, his left eye screwed shut. He kept staring at Alyosha.
"What's wrong? What trick?" Alyosha cried, thoroughly alarmed now.

"Why, look," the captain suddenly squealed, and showing him the two notes he'd been holding by one corner between thumb and forefinger throughout the conversation, he crumpled them up savagely and squeezed them tight in his right fist. "Do you see, do you see?" he shrieked, pale and furious. And suddenly flinging up his hand, he hurled the crumpled notes onto the sand. "Do you see?" he shrieked again, pointing at them. "Look there!"
And with wild fury he began stamping on them with his heel, gasping and shouting as he did:
"So much for your money! So much for your money! So much for your money! So much for your money!"
Suddenly he darted back and drew himself up in front of Alyosha, his whole frame radiating an unspeakable pride.

"Tell whoever sent you that the wisp of tow doesn't sell his honor," he cried, throwing his arm up in the air. Then he spun around and started to run; but he hadn't gone five steps before he turned completely around and blew Alyosha a kiss. He ran another five paces and then turned one last time. This time his face wasn't twisted with laughter, but shaking all over with tears. In a tearful, faltering, sobbing voice he cried:
"What would I say to my boy if I took money from you for our shame?"

And then he ran on without turning back. Alyosha watched him go, grieved beyond words. Oh, he understood now that until the very last moment the man himself hadn't known he was going to crumple up the notes and throw them away. He didn't turn back. Alyosha knew he wouldn't. He wouldn't run after him and call him back—he knew exactly why. Once the man was out of sight, Alyosha picked up the two notes. They were badly crushed and crumpled, pressed into the sand, but undamaged, and they even rustled like new ones when Alyosha unfolded them and smoothed them out. After smoothing them out, he folded them, put them in his pocket, and went to report to Katerina Ivanovna on how her errand had turned out.

title: I. The Engagement
paragraphs: Madame Khokhlakov was again the first to meet Alyosha. She was flustered; something important had happened. Katerina Ivanovna's hysterics had ended in a fainting fit, and then "a terrible, awful weakness followed—she lay with her eyes rolled up, delirious. Now she had a fever. They'd sent for Herzenstube, sent for the aunts. The aunts were already here, but Herzenstube hadn't come yet. Everyone was sitting in her room, waiting. She was unconscious now—what if it turned into brain fever!"

Madame Khokhlakov looked gravely alarmed. "This is serious, serious," she added after every sentence, as if nothing that had ever happened to her before had been serious. Alyosha listened, distressed, and began to describe his own adventures, but she cut him off at the first words. She had no time to listen. She begged him to sit with Lise and wait for her there.

"Lise," she whispered, almost in his ear, "Lise has greatly surprised me, just now, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch. She touched me too, and so my heart forgives her everything. Just imagine, the moment you'd gone, she became genuinely remorseful for having laughed at you today and yesterday—though she wasn't really laughing at you, only teasing. But she was truly sorry about it, almost in tears, so that I was quite astonished. She's never really been sorry for laughing at me, only turns it into a joke. And you know she's laughing at me practically every minute. But this time she meant it. She thinks a great deal of your opinion, Alexey Fyodorovitch, so don't take offense or feel hurt by her if you can help it. I'm never hard on her, because she's such a clever little thing. Would you believe it? She said just now that you were a friend of her childhood, 'the greatest friend of her childhood'—just imagine that—'greatest friend'—and what about me? She has very strong feelings and memories, and what's more, she uses the most unexpected phrases, words that come bursting out just when you least expect them. She was talking about a pine tree just recently, for instance: there used to be a pine tree standing in our garden back in her early childhood. Very likely it's still standing there, so there's no need to speak of it in the past tense. Pine trees aren't like people, Alexey Fyodorovitch, they don't change quickly. 'Mamma,' she said, 'I remember that pine tree the way you remember a dream'—only she put it in some far more original way that I can't repeat. Besides, I've forgotten it. Well, goodbye! I'm so worried I feel I'll lose my mind. Ah! Alexey Fyodorovitch, I've lost my mind twice in my life already. Go to Lise, cheer her up, the way you always can, so charmingly. Lise," she called out, heading to her door, "here, I've brought you Alexey Fyodorovitch, whom you insulted so badly. He's not the least bit angry, I assure you—on the contrary, he's surprised you could think such a thing."
"_Merci, maman._ Come in, Alexey Fyodorovitch."

Alyosha went in. Lise looked rather flustered, and blushed crimson at once. She was clearly embarrassed about something, and, as people always do in such cases, she immediately began talking about other things, as though they absorbed her completely at that moment.

"Mamma just told me the whole story of the two hundred rubles, Alexey Fyodorovitch, and how you took it to that poor officer... and she told me the whole dreadful story of how he'd been insulted... and you know, even though mamma muddles everything... jumps from one thing to another... I cried when I heard it. Well, did you give him the money, and how is that poor man doing now?"

"The truth is, I didn't give it to him, it's a long story," Alyosha answered, sounding as though he, too, could think of nothing but his regret at having failed—and Lise could see plainly enough that he, too, was looking away, that he, too, was trying to talk about other things.

Alyosha sat down at the table and began telling his story, but from the first few words his embarrassment fell away and he had Lise's full attention too. He spoke with deep feeling, still under the spell of the strong impression he'd just received, and he managed to tell the story well, in full detail. Back in Moscow he used to love coming to see Lise and describing whatever had just happened to him, what he'd been reading, or what he remembered from his childhood. Sometimes they'd made up daydreams together and spun whole little romances—usually cheerful, amusing ones. Now they both felt suddenly transported back to those old Moscow days, two years before. Lise was deeply moved by his story. Alyosha described Ilyusha with real warmth. When he finished describing how the unlucky man had trampled the money underfoot, Lise couldn't help clasping her hands and crying out:
"So you didn't give him the money! You let him run off! Oh dear, you should have run after him!"
"No, Lise, it's better that I didn't run after him," said Alyosha, getting up from his chair and pacing thoughtfully across the room.
"How so? How is that better? Now they're without food, and their situation is hopeless?"

"Not hopeless, because the two hundred rubles will still reach them. He'll take the money tomorrow. He's sure to take it tomorrow," said Alyosha, pacing back and forth, thinking it over. "You see, Lise," he went on, stopping suddenly in front of her, "I made one blunder, but even that blunder turns out to be all for the best."
"What blunder, and why is it for the best?"

"I'll tell you. He's a man of weak, timid character; he's suffered enormously, and he's very good-natured at heart. I keep asking myself why he took offense so suddenly, because I assure you, right up to the last minute, he had no idea he was going to trample on those notes. And now I think there was a great deal to offend him... it couldn't have been otherwise, given his situation.... To begin with, it stung him that he'd been so openly glad of the money in front of me, that he hadn't hidden it from me. If he'd been pleased, but not so much; if he hadn't shown it; if he'd started making a show of scruples and hesitation, the way other people do when accepting money, he might still have managed to take it. But he was too genuinely delighted, and that mortified him. Ah, Lise, he's a good, honest man—and that's the worst part of the whole business. The entire time he talked, his voice was so weak, so broken, he talked so fast, so fast, he kept laughing that laugh of his, or maybe he was crying—yes, I'm sure he was crying, he was so overjoyed—and he talked about his daughters—and about a position he might get in another town.... And once he'd poured his heart out, he felt ashamed of having bared his whole soul to me like that. So right away he began to hate me for it. He's one of those painfully sensitive poor people. What made him feel most ashamed was that he'd given in too quickly, accepted me as a friend, you see. At first he practically flew at me, tried to intimidate me, but the moment he saw the money he started embracing me, kept touching me with his hands. That's probably how it all came to feel so humiliating to him, and then I made that blunder, a very significant one. I suddenly told him that if he didn't have enough money to move to another town, we'd give him more, and that I myself would give him as much as he wanted, out of my own pocket. That hit him all at once. Why, he must have thought, did I push myself forward to help him? You know, Lise, it's awfully hard for a man who's been wronged when other people look at him as though they were his benefactors.... I've heard that—Father Zosima told me so. I don't quite know how to put it, but I've seen it myself, many times. And I feel it in myself too. And the worst of it is, though he didn't know, right up to the very last minute, that he'd trample on the notes, I'm sure he had some kind of premonition of it. That's exactly what put him in such ecstasy—having that premonition.... And even though it's dreadful, it's all for the best. In fact, I believe nothing better could have happened."
"Why, why could nothing better have happened?" cried Lise, staring at Alyosha in great astonishment.

"Because if he'd taken the money, an hour after getting home he'd have been crying with mortification—that's exactly what would have happened. And most likely he'd have come to see me first thing tomorrow, and maybe flung the notes at me and trampled them just like he did today. But as it is, he's gone home awfully proud and triumphant, even though he knows he's 'ruined himself.' So now nothing could be easier than to get him to accept the two hundred rubles by tomorrow, because he's already vindicated his honor, tossed the money away, trampled it underfoot.... He couldn't have known, when he did it, that I'd bring it to him again tomorrow, and yet he's in desperate need of that money. Even though he's proud of himself right now, today of all days he'll be thinking about how much help he's lost. He'll think about it even more tonight, he'll dream about it, and by tomorrow morning he might well be ready to come running to me to ask forgiveness. And that's exactly when I'll show up. 'Here,' I'll say, 'you're a proud man: you've proven it; now take the money and forgive us!' And then he'll take it!"
Alyosha was carried away with joy as he said those last words, "And then he'll take it!" Lise clapped her hands.
"Ah, that's true! I understand it perfectly now. Ah, Alyosha, how do you know all this? So young, and yet you know what's in the human heart.... I never would have worked that out."
"The main thing now is to convince him that he's on equal footing with us, despite taking money from us," Alyosha went on, still excited, "and not just equal—even on a higher footing."
"'On a higher footing' is a lovely way to put it, Alexey Fyodorovitch; but go on, go on!"
"You mean there's no such expression as 'on a higher footing'—but that doesn't matter, because—"

"Oh, no, of course it doesn't matter. Forgive me, Alyosha, dear.... You know, until now I scarcely respected you—that is, I respected you, but only on equal footing; but from now on I'll respect you on a higher footing. Don't be angry, dear, at my joking," she added at once, with real feeling. "I'm absurd and small, but you, you! Listen, Alexey Fyodorovitch. Isn't there something in all this analysis—I mean your analysis... no, let's call it ours—aren't we showing contempt for him, for that poor man, by dissecting his soul like this, as it were, from above? In deciding so confidently that he'll take the money?"

"No, Lise, it's not contempt," Alyosha answered, as if he'd braced himself for that very question. "I was thinking about that on the way here. How could it be contempt, when we're all just like him, all exactly the same as he is? Because you know, we really are the same, no better than him. If we're better in some way, we'd still have been exactly like him in his position.... I don't know about you, Lise, but I consider my own soul sordid in a lot of ways, while his soul isn't sordid at all—quite the opposite, it's full of fine feeling.... No, Lise, I don't feel contempt for him. Do you know, Lise, my elder once told me to care for most people exactly as one would for children, and for some of them the way one cares for patients in a hospital."
"Ah, Alexey Fyodorovitch, dear, let's care for people the way we'd care for the sick!"
"Let's, Lise; I'm ready. Though I'm not entirely ready within myself. I'm sometimes very impatient, and other times I just don't see things clearly. It's different with you."
"Ah, I don't believe that! Alexey Fyodorovitch, how happy I am!"
"I'm so glad you say that, Lise."

"Alexey Fyodorovitch, you're wonderfully good, but you're sometimes a bit stiff.... And yet you're not the least bit stiff, really. Go to the door, open it quietly, and see if mamma is listening," Lise said in a nervous, rushed whisper.
Alyosha went, opened the door, and reported that no one was listening.

"Come here, Alexey Fyodorovitch," Lise went on, blushing redder and redder. "Give me your hand—there. I have to make a big confession—I didn't write to you yesterday as a joke, I meant it seriously," and she covered her eyes with her hand. It was obvious she was deeply ashamed of the confession.
Suddenly she snatched his hand and impulsively kissed it three times.
"Ah, Lise, how wonderful!" Alyosha cried happily. "You know, I was completely certain you meant it."
"Certain? Honestly!" She pushed his hand aside, but didn't let go of it, blushing furiously, laughing a small, happy laugh. "I kiss his hand and he says, 'How wonderful!'"
But her complaint wasn't fair. Alyosha, too, was deeply moved.
"I'd like to please you always, Lise, but I don't know how to go about it," he mumbled, blushing too.

"Alyosha, dear, you're cold and rude. See? He's already chosen me for his wife and has it all settled in his mind. He's sure I meant it seriously. What a thing to say! Why, that's downright impertinence—that's what it is."
"Why, was it wrong of me to be sure?" Alyosha asked, suddenly laughing.
"Ah, Alyosha, quite the opposite—it was wonderfully right," cried Lise, looking at him tenderly and happily.
Alyosha stood still, holding her hand in his. Suddenly he bent down and kissed her on the lips.
"Oh, what are you doing?" cried Lise. Alyosha was terribly embarrassed.
"Oh, forgive me if I shouldn't have.... Maybe I'm being awfully stupid.... You said I was cold, so I kissed you.... But now I see it was stupid."
Lise laughed and hid her face in her hands. "And in that outfit!" she blurted out in the middle of her laughter. But then she suddenly stopped laughing and grew serious, almost stern.

"Alyosha, we have to put off the kissing. We're not ready for that yet, and we'll have a long time to wait," she finished abruptly. "Tell me instead—why does someone as clever, as intelligent, as observant as you choose a little idiot, an invalid like me? Ah, Alyosha, I'm terribly happy, because I don't deserve you in the least."

"You do, Lise. I'll be leaving the monastery for good in a few days. If I go out into the world, I have to marry. I know that. He told me to marry too. Who could I marry better than you—and who would even have me besides you? I've thought it over. First of all, you've known me since I was a child, and you have plenty of qualities I lack. You're more lighthearted than I am; above all, you're more innocent than I am. I've already come into contact with far too many things.... Ah, you don't know it, but I'm a Karamazov too. So what if you laugh and joke, and make fun of me too? Go on laughing. I'm glad you do. You laugh like a little child, but you think like someone who's suffered."
"Like someone who's suffered? How so?"

"Yes, Lise, that question of yours a moment ago—whether we weren't showing contempt for that poor man by dissecting his soul—that was the question of someone who's known suffering.... I don't quite know how to put it, but anyone who thinks about questions like that is capable of suffering themselves. Sitting in that invalid chair of yours, you must have already thought over a great deal."

"Alyosha, give me your hand. Why are you pulling it away?" Lise murmured, her voice failing, weak with happiness. "Listen, Alyosha. What will you wear when you leave the monastery? What kind of suit? Don't laugh, don't get angry, it matters a great deal to me, a great deal."
"I haven't thought about the suit, Lise, but I'll wear whatever you like."
"I'd like you in a dark blue velvet coat, a white piqué waistcoat, and a soft gray felt hat.... Tell me, did you believe I didn't care for you, when I said I didn't mean what I'd written?"
"No, I didn't believe it."
"Oh, you impossible person, you're incorrigible."
"You see, I knew that you—seemed to care for me, but I pretended to believe you didn't, to make it—easier for you."

"That makes it worse! Worse and better than anything! Alyosha, I'm terribly fond of you. Just before you arrived this morning, I told my own fortune. I decided I'd ask you for my letter, and if you pulled it out calmly and just handed it back (which is exactly what one would expect of you), it would mean you didn't care for me at all, that you felt nothing, that you were simply a foolish boy, good for nothing, and that I was ruined. But you'd left the letter at home, and that cheered me up. You left it behind on purpose, so you wouldn't have to give it back, because you knew I'd ask for it? That was it, wasn't it?"
"Ah, Lise, it wasn't like that at all. The letter's with me right now, it was this morning too, right here in this pocket. Here it is."
Alyosha pulled the letter out, laughing, and held it up to show her, but out of reach.
"But I'm not going to give it to you. Look at it from over there."
"So then you lied? You, a monk, told a lie!"

"I told a lie, if you want to call it that," Alyosha laughed too. "I lied so I wouldn't have to give the letter back. It's very precious to me," he added suddenly, with real feeling, and blushed again. "It always will be, and I won't hand it over to anyone!"
Lise looked at him happily. "Alyosha," she murmured again, "look at the door. Isn't mamma listening?"
"All right, Lise, I'll look; but wouldn't it be better not to? Why suspect your mother of something so petty?"

"What's petty about it? Her keeping an eye on her own daughter is her right, it's not petty at all!" Lise flared up. "You can be sure, Alexey Fyodorovitch, that when I'm a mother, if I have a daughter like myself, I will absolutely spy on her!"
"Really, Lise? That's not right."

"Oh, good heavens! What does pettiness have to do with it? If she were listening in on some ordinary worldly conversation, that would be petty, but when her own daughter is shut up alone with a young man.... Listen, Alyosha, do you know I'm going to spy on you the moment we're married, and let me tell you, I'll open all your letters and read every one, so you might as well be prepared."
"Yes, of course, if that's how it is—" Alyosha mumbled, "only it's not right."

"Ah, how contemptuous! Alyosha dear, let's not quarrel on the very first day. I'd better tell you the whole truth. Of course it's very wrong to spy on people, and of course I'm the one in the wrong and you're right, only I'm going to spy on you regardless."
"Go ahead then; you won't find anything out," laughed Alyosha.
"And, Alyosha, will you defer to me? We need to settle that too."
"I'll be glad to, Lise, and I certainly will, only not in the most important things. Even if you don't agree with me, I'll do my duty when it comes to the most important things."

"That's right; but let me tell you, I'm ready to defer to you not only in the most important matters, but in everything. And I'm ready to vow it right now—everything, for the rest of my life!" Lise cried fervently. "And I'll do it gladly, gladly! What's more, I swear I'll never spy on you, not once, never read a single one of your letters. Because you're right about it and I'm not. And even though I'll be terribly tempted to spy, I know I won't, since you consider it dishonorable. You're my conscience now.... Listen, Alexey Fyodorovitch, why have you been so sad lately—both yesterday and today? I know you have plenty of worries and troubles, but I can see you have some special grief besides, maybe a secret one?"
"Yes, Lise, I do have a secret one too," Alyosha answered sorrowfully. "I can see you love me, since you guessed that."
"What grief? About what? Can you tell me?" Lise asked, with timid pleading.
"I'll tell you later, Lise—afterward," said Alyosha, flustered. "You might not understand it now, and maybe I couldn't even explain it properly."
"I know your brothers and your father are troubling you too."
"Yes, my brothers too," Alyosha murmured, lost in thought.
"I don't like your brother Ivan, Alyosha," Lise said suddenly.
He noted this remark with some surprise, but didn't answer it.

"My brothers are destroying themselves," he went on, "my father too. And they're destroying others along with them. It's 'the primitive force of the Karamazovs,' as Father Paissy said the other day—a crude, unbridled, earthly force. Does the spirit of God move above that force? Even that, I don't know. I only know that I'm a Karamazov too.... Me, a monk, a monk! Am I really a monk, Lise? You said so just now."
"Yes, I did."
"And maybe I don't even believe in God."

"You don't believe? What's wrong?" Lise said quietly, gently. But Alyosha didn't answer. There was something too mysterious, too deeply personal in these last words of his, perhaps obscure even to himself, and yet tormenting him.

"And now, on top of everything, my friend, the best man in the world, is leaving, leaving the earth! If you knew, Lise, how bound up my soul is with his! And then I'll be alone.... I'll come to you, Lise.... From now on we'll be together."
"Yes, together, together! From now on we'll always be together, our whole lives! Listen, kiss me, I'm allowing it."
Alyosha kissed her.

"Come now, go. Christ be with you!" and she made the sign of the cross over him. "Hurry back to him while he's still alive. I see I've kept you here far too cruelly. I'll pray today for him and for you. Alyosha, we're going to be happy! Are we going to be happy, are we?"
"I believe we will, Lise."

Alyosha thought it best not to go in to see Madame Khokhlakov and was heading out of the house without saying goodbye to her. But no sooner had he opened the door than he found Madame Khokhlakov standing right in front of him. From her very first word, Alyosha guessed she'd been waiting there on purpose to catch him.

"Alexey Fyodorovitch, this is dreadful. This is all childish nonsense and ridiculous. I trust you're not dreaming of— It's foolishness, nothing but foolishness!" she said, launching straight into him.
"Just don't say that to her," said Alyosha, "or she'll get upset, and that's bad for her right now."
"Sensible advice from a sensible young man. Am I to understand that you only agreed with her out of pity for her invalid condition, because you didn't want to upset her by contradicting her?"
"Oh, no, not at all. I was completely serious about what I said," Alyosha declared firmly.
"Being serious about it is impossible, unthinkable, and in the first place, I will never be at home to you again, and I'll take her away, you can be sure of that."
"But why?" asked Alyosha. "It's all so far off. We might have to wait another year and a half."

"Ah, Alexey Fyodorovitch, that's true, of course, and you'll have plenty of time to quarrel and split up a thousand times over in a year and a half. But I'm so unhappy! Even though it's such nonsense, it's a terrible blow to me. I feel like Famusov in the last scene of Woe from Wit. You're Chatsky and she's Sophia, and only imagine, I ran down to meet you right on the stairs, and in the play the fatal scene happens on the staircase too. I heard everything, I nearly collapsed. So this is what explains her dreadful night and her hysterics lately! It means love for the daughter, but death for the mother. I might as well lie down in my grave right now. And more serious still, what is that letter she wrote? Show it to me this instant, this instant!"
"No, there's no need. Tell me instead, how is Katerina Ivanovna now? I have to know."

"She's still lying there delirious; she hasn't regained consciousness. Her aunts are here, but all they do is sigh and put on airs. Herzenstube came, and he was so alarmed I didn't know what to do for him. I nearly sent for a doctor to look after him. He had to be driven home in my carriage. And on top of it all, you and this letter! It's true, nothing can happen for a year and a half. In the name of everything holy, in the name of your dying elder, show me that letter, Alexey Fyodorovitch. I'm her mother. Hold it in your own hand if you like, and I'll read it that way."
"No, I won't show it to you. Even if she gave me permission, I wouldn't. I'll come tomorrow, and if you like, we can talk over plenty of things then, but for now, goodbye!"
And Alyosha ran downstairs and out into the street.

title: II. Smerdyakov With A Guitar
paragraphs: He really had no time to lose. Even while saying goodbye to Lise, it had struck him that he needed to come up with some kind of scheme to track down his brother Dmitri, who was clearly avoiding him. It was getting late, nearly three o'clock. Alyosha's whole soul was pulling him back to the monastery, to his dying saint, but the need to see Dmitri outweighed everything else. The conviction that some great, unavoidable catastrophe was about to happen grew stronger in Alyosha's mind with every passing hour. What exactly that catastrophe would be, and what he would say to his brother at that moment, he probably couldn't have said with any certainty. "Even if my benefactor has to die without me there, at least I won't have to spend the rest of my life reproaching myself with the thought that I might have saved something and didn't—that I walked past and hurried home instead. If I do what I mean to do now, I'll be following his great teaching."

His plan was to catch his brother Dmitri unawares—to climb over the fence, as he had the day before, slip into the garden, and sit in the summer house. If Dmitri wasn't there, Alyosha thought, he wouldn't announce himself to Foma or the women of the house, but would stay hidden in the summer house, even if it meant waiting there until evening. If, as before, Dmitri were lying in wait for Grushenka to show up, he'd very likely come to the summer house himself. Alyosha didn't dwell much on the details of his plan, though; he simply resolved to act on it, even if it meant not getting back to the monastery that day.

Everything went smoothly; he climbed over the fence almost at the exact spot as the day before, and slipped into the summer house unseen. He didn't want to be noticed. The woman of the house, and Foma too, if he was around, might well be loyal to his brother and follow his instructions, refusing to let Alyosha into the garden, or might warn Dmitri that someone was looking for him.

There was no one in the summer house. Alyosha sat down and began to wait. He looked around the summer house, which somehow struck him as much older than it had seemed the day before. Though the day was every bit as fine as yesterday, this time the place seemed a shabby little spot. There was a ring on the table, no doubt left by the glass of brandy spilled the day before. Foolish, irrelevant thoughts drifted through his mind, as they always do during a tedious wait. He found himself wondering, for instance, why he'd sat down in exactly the same spot as before, rather than somewhere else. At last he began to feel quite low—weighed down by suspense and uncertainty. But he hadn't been sitting there more than a quarter of an hour when he suddenly heard the strum of a guitar somewhere close by. People were sitting, or had just sat down, in the bushes no more than twenty paces off. Alyosha suddenly remembered that on his way out of the summer house the day before, he'd caught a glimpse of an old, low, green garden bench among the bushes to the left, by the fence. The people must be sitting there now. Who were they?
A man's voice suddenly started singing in a sugary falsetto, accompanying himself on the guitar:
With a force no one can master I am bound fast to my dear. O Lord, have mercy On her and on me! On her and on me! On her and on me!
The voice stopped. It was a lackey's tenor, and a lackey's song. Another voice, a woman's, asked suddenly, coyly and insinuatingly, with a kind of prim affectation:
"Why haven't you come to see us in so long, Pavel Fyodorovitch? Why do you always look down on us?"

"Not at all," a man's voice answered politely, but with pointed dignity. It was clear the man had the upper hand here, and that the woman was the one making advances. "That must be Smerdyakov," Alyosha thought, "going by the voice. And the lady must be the daughter of the house, the one who came back from Moscow, who wears the dress with a train and goes to Marfa for her soup."
"I'm terribly fond of verses of all kinds, as long as they rhyme," the woman's voice went on. "Why don't you go on?"
The man sang again:
What do I care for royal treasure If my dear one's well, at leisure? Lord have mercy On her and on me! On her and on me! On her and on me!
"It sounded even better last time," the woman's voice observed. "You sang 'If my darling's well and gay'—it sounded more tender. I suppose you've forgotten it today."
"Poetry is rubbish!" Smerdyakov said curtly.
"Oh, no! I'm very fond of poetry."

"As far as it's poetry, it's essentially rubbish. Think about it yourself—who ever actually talks in rhyme? And if we all had to talk in rhyme, even if the government decreed it, we wouldn't get much said, would we? Poetry's no good, Marya Kondratyevna."
"How clever you are! However did you come to think so deeply about everything?" The woman's voice grew more and more coaxing.

"I could have done far better than this. I could have known a great deal more than I do, if it weren't for my fate ever since childhood. I would have shot a man in a duel if he'd insulted me for being descended from a filthy beggar woman with no father to speak of. And they used to throw that in my face, even in Moscow. It reached them from here, thanks to Grigory Vassilyevitch. Grigory Vassilyevitch blames me for rebelling against my own birth, but I would have consented to being killed before I was ever born, rather than come into this world at all. They used to say, in the marketplace, and your own mamma too, with no delicacy whatsoever, went out of her way to tell me that her hair looked like a doormat and that she was five foot minus a tiny bit. Why say 'a tiny bit' when she could have just said 'a little bit,' like everyone else? She wanted to make it sound touching—pure peasant sentiment. Can a Russian peasant really be said to feel anything, compared to an educated man? He can't be said to have real feeling at all, given his ignorance. Ever since childhood, whenever I hear someone say 'a tiny bit,' I could burst with rage. I hate the whole of Russia, Marya Kondratyevna."
"If you'd been a cadet in the army, or a young hussar, you wouldn't talk like that—you'd have drawn your saber to defend all of Russia."
"I don't want to be a hussar, Marya Kondratyevna, and what's more, I'd like to see all soldiers abolished."
"And when an enemy comes, who's going to defend us then?"

"There's no need of defense. In 1812 there was a great invasion of Russia by Napoleon, first Emperor of the French, father of the current one, and it would have been a good thing if they'd conquered us. A clever nation would have conquered a very stupid one and annexed it. We'd have entirely different institutions now."

"Are things really so much better in their own country than they are here? I wouldn't trade one dandy I know for three young Englishmen," Marya Kondratyevna remarked tenderly, no doubt accompanying her words with a most languishing glance.
"That's a matter of preference."
"But you're just like a foreigner yourself—just like a proper, gentlemanly foreigner. I'll say it, even though it makes me blush."

"If you want to know, the folks over there and the ones here are exactly alike in their vices. They're all swindlers—it's just that over there the scoundrel wears polished boots, and here he grovels in the muck and sees nothing wrong with it. The Russian people need a good thrashing, just as Fyodor Pavlovitch said very truly yesterday, even though he's mad, and so are all his children."
"You said yourself you had such respect for Ivan Fyodorovitch."

"But he called me a stinking lackey. He thinks I might turn unruly. He's wrong about that. If I had a certain sum of money in my pocket, I'd have left this place long ago. Dmitri Fyodorovitch is lower than any lackey—in his behavior, in his mind, and in his poverty. He doesn't know how to do a single thing, and yet everyone respects him. I may be only a cook, but with a bit of luck I could open a café-restaurant on Petrovka Street in Moscow, because my cooking is something special, and there's no one in Moscow, besides the foreigners, whose cooking is anything special at all. Dmitri Fyodorovitch is a beggar, but if he challenged the son of the first count in the land, he'd fight him. Yet how exactly is he better than I am? He's far, far stupider than I am. Just look at the money he's thrown away for no reason at all!"
"A duel must be a wonderful thing," Marya Kondratyevna remarked suddenly.
"How so?"

"It must be so terrifying and so brave, especially when young officers with pistols in hand fire at each other over some lady. A perfect picture! Ah, if only girls were allowed to watch, I'd give anything to see one!"
"It's all very well when you're the one firing at someone else, but when he's firing straight at your face, you'll feel pretty foolish. You'd be glad to run away, Marya Kondratyevna."
"You don't mean to say you would run away?" But Smerdyakov didn't deign to answer. After a moment of silence, the guitar tinkled again, and he sang once more in the same falsetto:
Whatever you may say, I'm bound to go away. Life will be bright and gay In the city far away. I shall not grieve, I shall not grieve at all, I don't intend to grieve at all.

Then something unexpected happened. Alyosha suddenly sneezed. They fell silent. Alyosha got up and walked toward them. He found Smerdyakov all dressed up, wearing polished boots, his hair pomaded and perhaps even curled. The guitar lay on the garden bench. His companion was the daughter of the house, wearing a pale-blue dress with a train two yards long. She was young, and wouldn't have been bad-looking if her face hadn't been so round and so badly freckled.
"Will my brother Dmitri be back soon?" Alyosha asked, with as much composure as he could manage.
Smerdyakov got up slowly; Marya Kondratyevna rose too.
"How would I know about Dmitri Fyodorovitch? It's not as though I'm his keeper," Smerdyakov answered, quietly, distinctly, and with a hint of condescension.
"But I only asked whether you happen to know," Alyosha explained.
"I have no idea where he is, and I have no wish to know."
"But my brother told me you keep him informed of everything that goes on in the house, and that you promised to let him know when Agrafena Alexandrovna arrives."
Smerdyakov turned an unhurried, unruffled gaze on him.
"And how did you get in this time, since the gate's been bolted for an hour now?" he asked, looking at Alyosha.
"I came in from the back alley, over the fence, and went straight to the summer house. I hope you'll forgive me," he added, turning to Marya Kondratyevna. "I was in a hurry to find my brother."

"Ach, as if we'd hold it against you!" Marya Kondratyevna drawled, flattered by Alyosha's apology. "Because Dmitri Fyodorovitch often comes to the summer house that same way. We don't even know he's here, and there he is, sitting in the summer house."
"I'm very anxious to find him, or at least to learn from you where he might be now. Believe me, it's a matter of great importance to him."
"He never tells us anything," Marya Kondratyevna lisped.

"Though I used to come by here as a friend," Smerdyakov began again, "Dmitri Fyodorovitch has hounded me mercilessly, even here, with his endless questions about the master. 'Any news?' he'll ask. 'What's going on in there now? Who's coming and going?' as if I couldn't tell him something more useful. Twice already he's threatened to kill me."
"To kill you?" Alyosha exclaimed, startled.

"Do you suppose that would trouble him much, given his temper, which you had a chance to observe for yourself yesterday? He says if I let Agrafena Alexandrovna in and she spends the night there, I'll be the first one to suffer for it. I'm terribly afraid of him, and if I weren't even more afraid of doing it, I really ought to let the police know. God alone knows what he might do."
"His honor told him the other day, 'I'll grind you up in a mortar!'" Marya Kondratyevna added.
"Oh, if it's only grinding him up in a mortar, that might just be talk," Alyosha observed. "If I could meet him, I might have a word with him about that too."

"Well, the only thing I can tell you is this," said Smerdyakov, as though reconsidering, "I come here as an old friend and neighbor, so it wouldn't be strange if I didn't visit. But on the other hand, first thing this morning Ivan Fyodorovitch sent me to your brother's lodgings on Lake Street, with no letter, just a message for Dmitri Fyodorovitch to come dine with him at the restaurant here, in the marketplace. I went, but didn't find Dmitri Fyodorovitch at home, even though it was eight o'clock. 'He was here, but he's gone off entirely,' his landlady told me, in those exact words. It's almost as if there was some understanding between the two of them. Maybe at this very moment he's at the restaurant with Ivan Fyodorovitch, because Ivan Fyodorovitch hasn't been home for dinner, and Fyodor Pavlovitch dined alone an hour ago and has gone to lie down. But I beg you most particularly not to mention me, or anything I've told you, because he'd kill me over nothing at all."
"Brother Ivan invited Dmitri to the restaurant today?" Alyosha repeated quickly.
"That's right."
"The Metropolis tavern, in the marketplace?"
"The very same."
"That's quite possible," Alyosha cried, greatly excited. "Thank you, Smerdyakov, that's important. I'll go there right away."
"Don't give me away," Smerdyakov called after him.
"Oh, no, I'll go to the tavern as though I just happened by. Don't worry."
"But wait a moment, I'll open the gate for you," Marya Kondratyevna called.
"No, it's a shortcut, I'll go back over the fence."

What he'd just heard threw Alyosha into a state of great agitation. He ran to the tavern. He couldn't very well walk into the tavern in his monastic robes, but he could ask at the entrance for his brothers and call them down.
