But just as he reached the tavern, a window flew open, and his brother Ivan called down to him from it.
"Alyosha, can't you come up here to me? I'd be awfully grateful."
"Of course I can, only I'm not quite sure whether in this outfit—"
"But I'm in a private room. Come up the stairs; I'll run down to meet you."
A minute later Alyosha was sitting beside his brother. Ivan was dining alone.

title: III. The Brothers Make Friends
paragraphs: Ivan, though, wasn't in a separate room, only behind a screen that kept him hidden from the rest of the room. It was the first room off the entrance, with a buffet counter along the wall. Waiters kept darting back and forth through it. The only other customer in the room was an old retired army man drinking tea in a corner. But there was the usual racket coming from the other rooms of the tavern—shouts for waiters, the pop of corks, the click of billiard balls, the drone of a barrel organ. Alyosha knew Ivan didn't usually come to this tavern and disliked taverns in general. So he must have come here, Alyosha reasoned, simply to meet Dmitri by arrangement. And yet Dmitri wasn't there.
"Shall I order you fish, soup, something? You can't live on tea alone, I suppose," Ivan cried, clearly delighted to have caught hold of Alyosha. He'd finished his dinner and was drinking tea.
"Let me have soup, and tea after, I'm hungry," Alyosha said cheerfully.
"And cherry jam? They have it here. Remember how you used to love cherry jam when you were little?"
"You remember that? Let me have jam too, I still like it."
Ivan rang for the waiter and ordered soup, jam, and tea.

"I remember everything, Alyosha, I remember you up until you were eleven—I was nearly fifteen. There's such a gap between fifteen and eleven that brothers are never really companions at those ages. I don't even know if I was fond of you back then. When I first went off to Moscow, I never thought about you at all for the first few years. Then, when you came to Moscow yourself, I believe we only met once, somewhere. And now I've been here more than three months, and so far we've barely said two words to each other. I'm leaving tomorrow, and I was just sitting here thinking how I might see you to say goodbye, and just then you walked by."
"Were you so anxious to see me, then?"

"Very. I want to get to know you once and for all, and I want you to know me. And then say goodbye. I think it's always best to get to know people right before you part from them. I've noticed how you've been looking at me these past three months. There's been a constant look of expectation in your eyes, and I can't stand that. That's why I've kept my distance from you. But in the end I've come to respect you. The little man stands firm, I thought. Though I'm laughing as I say it, I mean it seriously. You really do stand firm, don't you? I like people who hold firm to something, whatever it is, even when they're as small as you are. Your expectant eyes stopped annoying me—I grew fond of them, eventually, those expectant eyes of yours. You seem to love me, for some reason, Alyosha?"

"I do love you, Ivan. Dmitri says of you—Ivan is a grave. I say of you—Ivan is a riddle. You're still a riddle to me, even now. But I understand something about you, something I didn't understand until this morning."
"What's that?" Ivan laughed.
"You won't be angry?" Alyosha laughed too.
"Well?"
"That you're every bit as young as other young men of twenty-three, that you're simply a young, fresh, decent boy, green, in fact! Now, have I insulted you terribly?"

"On the contrary, I'm struck by a coincidence," Ivan cried, warmly and good-naturedly. "Would you believe it, ever since that scene with her, I've thought of nothing but my own youthful greenness, and here you are, as if you'd guessed it, bringing it up yourself. Do you know, I've been sitting here thinking to myself: even if I stopped believing in life, if I lost faith in the woman I love, lost faith in the order of things, became convinced, in fact, that everything is a disorderly, damnable, maybe even devil-ridden chaos, even if I were struck by every horror of human disillusionment—I'd still want to live, and having once put the cup to my lips, I wouldn't turn away from it until I'd drained it dry! At thirty, though, I'll surely set the cup down, even unfinished, and turn away—to where, I don't know. But until I'm thirty, I know my youth will win out over everything—every disillusionment, every disgust with life. I've asked myself many times whether there's any despair in the world that could overpower this frantic, maybe unseemly thirst for life in me, and I've concluded there isn't—not until I'm thirty, anyway, and then I imagine I'll lose it on my own. Some sniveling, consumptive moralists—poets especially—often call that thirst for life base. It's a Karamazov trait, true enough, that thirst for life regardless of everything; you probably have it too, no doubt, but why call it base? The centripetal force on this planet of ours is still terribly strong, Alyosha. I have a longing for life, and I go on living in spite of logic. Even if I don't believe in the order of the universe, I still love the sticky little leaves as they unfurl in spring. I love the blue sky, I love certain people, whom one loves, you know, sometimes without knowing why. I love certain great deeds done by men, even though I may have long since stopped believing in them, my heart still prizes them out of old habit. Here, they've brought your soup, eat it, it'll do you good. It's excellent soup, they know how to make it here. I want to travel through Europe, Alyosha, I'll set off from here. And yet I know I'm only going to a graveyard, but it's a most precious graveyard, that's the thing! Precious are the dead who lie there, every stone over them speaks of such burning life in the past, such passionate faith in their work, their truth, their struggle, their science, that I know I'll fall to the ground and kiss those stones and weep over them—even though in my heart I'm convinced it's long since become nothing but a graveyard. And I won't weep out of despair, but simply because I'll be happy in my tears, I'll steep my soul in that emotion. I love the sticky leaves in spring, the blue sky—that's really all it is. It's not a matter of intellect or logic, it's loving with one's insides, with one's gut. One loves the first raw strength of one's youth. Do you understand any of this rant of mine, Alyosha?" Ivan suddenly laughed.

"I understand it all too well, Ivan. One longs to love with one's insides, with one's gut. You put that beautifully, and I'm so glad you have such a longing for life," Alyosha cried. "I think everyone ought to love life above everything else in the world."
"Love life more than its meaning?"

"Absolutely—love it regardless of logic, as you say, it has to be regardless of logic, and only then will one understand its meaning. I've thought that for a long time. Half your work is already done, Ivan, you love life—now you just have to try for the second half, and you'll be saved."
"You're trying to save me, but maybe I'm not lost at all! And what does this second half of yours mean?"
"Why, one has to raise up your dead, who perhaps haven't died after all. Come, let me have my tea. I'm so glad of this talk, Ivan."
"I can see you're feeling inspired. I'm awfully fond of these professions of faith from—novices, like you. You're a steadfast sort, Alexey. Is it true you mean to leave the monastery?"
"Yes, my elder is sending me out into the world."

"Then we'll see each other out there, in the world. We'll meet again before I turn thirty, when I'll start turning away from the cup. Father doesn't want to turn away from his cup until he's seventy—he dreams of hanging on until eighty, in fact, or so he says. He means it far too seriously, buffoon though he is. He too stands on solid rock—he stands on his own sensuality—though once we're past thirty, there may genuinely be nothing else left to stand on.... But hanging on until seventy is disgusting; better to stop at thirty; one might still keep 'a shadow of nobility' by deceiving oneself. Have you seen Dmitri today?"
"No, but I saw Smerdyakov," and Alyosha quickly, though in careful detail, described his meeting with Smerdyakov. Ivan started listening anxiously and began questioning him.
"But he begged me not to tell Dmitri that he'd told me about him," Alyosha added. Ivan frowned and fell into thought.
"Are you frowning on Smerdyakov's account?" Alyosha asked.
"Yes, on his account. Damn him, I did want to see Dmitri, but there's no need now," Ivan said reluctantly.
"But are you really leaving so soon, brother?"
"Yes."
"What about Dmitri and father—how will it all end?" Alyosha asked anxiously.

"You keep harping on that! What business is it of mine? Am I my brother Dmitri's keeper?" Ivan snapped irritably, then suddenly smiled bitterly. "That's Cain's answer about his murdered brother, isn't it? Maybe that's what you're thinking right now? Well, damn it all, I can't stay here to be their keeper, can I? I've finished what I came to do, and I'm leaving. Do you imagine I'm jealous of Dmitri, that I've been trying to steal his lovely Katerina Ivanovna for the last three months? Nonsense, I had business of my own to settle. I've finished it. I'm leaving. I finished it just now—you were there to see it."
"At Katerina Ivanovna's?"

"Yes, and I've freed myself once and for all. And really, what business is it of mine, Dmitri's? Dmitri doesn't even come into it. I had my own affairs to settle with Katerina Ivanovna. You know perfectly well, on the other hand, that Dmitri behaved as though there were some understanding between us. I never asked him to do that, but he solemnly handed her over to me and gave us his blessing. It's all too absurd. Ah, Alyosha, if only you knew how light my heart feels now! Would you believe it, I sat here eating my dinner and nearly ordered champagne to celebrate my first hour of freedom. Pah! It went on for nearly six months, and all at once I've thrown it off. I couldn't have guessed, even yesterday, how easy it would be to put an end to it, once I actually wanted to."
"You're talking about your love, Ivan?"

"My love, if you like. I fell in love with the young lady, fretted over her, and she fretted over me. I sat there keeping watch over her... and then all at once it collapsed! I spoke with real inspiration this morning, but once I left I burst out laughing. Would you believe it? Yes, it's the literal truth."
"You seem quite merry about it now," Alyosha observed, studying his face, which had suddenly brightened.

"But how was I supposed to know I didn't care for her in the least! Ha ha! Turns out I didn't, after all. And yet how she drew me in! How attractive she was, just now, while I was making my little speech! And you know, she still draws me in terribly, even now, and yet how easy it is to walk away from her. You think I'm bragging?"
"No, maybe it just wasn't love."

"Alyosha," Ivan laughed, "don't go philosophizing about love, it doesn't suit you. How you threw yourself into that discussion this morning! I forgot to kiss you for it.... But how she tormented me! It really was like sitting beside a 'laceration.' Ah, she knew perfectly well how much I loved her! She loved me, not Dmitri," Ivan insisted cheerfully. "Her feeling for Dmitri was pure self-laceration. Everything I told her just now was absolutely true, but the worst of it is, it might take her fifteen or twenty years to realize she doesn't care for Dmitri at all, and loves me instead, the one she torments, and maybe she'll never realize it, despite today's lesson. Well, it's better this way; I can simply walk away for good. By the way, how is she now? What happened after I left?"
Alyosha told him she'd had hysterics, and that now, from what he'd heard, she was unconscious and delirious.
"Isn't Madame Khokhlakov exaggerating?"
"I don't think so."
"I ought to find out. But no one dies from hysterics, anyway. They don't matter. God gave women hysterics as a kind of relief. I won't go see her at all. Why push myself forward again?"
"But you told her she'd never cared for you."
"I did that on purpose. Alyosha, shall I order some champagne? Let's drink to my freedom. Ah, if only you knew how glad I am!"
"No, brother, better not drink," Alyosha said suddenly. "Besides, I feel somehow low."
"Yes, you've been low for a while, I've noticed it."
"So you've decided to leave tomorrow morning, then?"

"Morning? I never said I'd leave in the morning.... But maybe it will be the morning. Would you believe it, I only dined here today to avoid dining with the old man, I loathe him so much. As far as he's concerned, I should have left long ago. But why are you so worried about my leaving? We've got plenty of time before I go—an eternity!"
"If you're leaving tomorrow, what do you mean by an eternity?"

"But what does it matter to us?" Ivan laughed. "We've got time enough for our talk, for what brought us here. Why do you look so surprised? Answer me: why did we meet here? To talk about my love for Katerina Ivanovna, about the old man and Dmitri? About foreign travel? About the fatal state of Russia? About the Emperor Napoleon? Is that it?"
"No."

"Then you know why. It's different for other people, but we, in our green youth, have to settle the eternal questions first of all. That's what matters to us. Young Russia does nothing but talk about the eternal questions these days. Just when the older generation has thrown itself into practical concerns. Why have you been looking at me with that expectant look for the last three months? To ask me, 'What do you believe, or don't you believe at all?' Isn't that what your eyes have been asking, these three months?"
"Perhaps so," Alyosha smiled. "You're not laughing at me now, are you, Ivan?"

"Me, laughing! I don't want to wound my little brother, who's been watching me with such expectation for three months. Alyosha, look straight at me! Of course, I'm just as much a little boy as you are, only not a novice. And what have Russian boys been up to, up until now—some of them, anyway? Take this reeking tavern, for instance—they meet here and sit down in a corner. They've never met once in their lives before, and once they leave the tavern, they won't meet again for forty years. And what do they talk about, in that brief pause in the tavern? The eternal questions—whether God exists, whether there's immortality. And the ones who don't believe in God talk about socialism or anarchism instead, about remaking the whole of humanity on some new pattern—which amounts to the same thing, really, the same questions turned inside out. And masses, masses of the most original Russian boys do nothing but talk about the eternal questions! Isn't that so?"

"Yes, for real Russians, the question of whether God exists, and of immortality—or, as you put it, the same questions turned inside out—comes first and foremost, of course, and it should," said Alyosha, still watching his brother with that same gentle, questioning smile.

"Well, Alyosha, sometimes it's very unwise to be Russian at all, but it's hard to imagine anything stupider than the way Russian boys spend their time. Still, there's one Russian boy named Alyosha I'm awfully fond of."
"How nicely you put that!" Alyosha suddenly laughed.
"Well, tell me where to start, give the orders. The existence of God, eh?"
"Start wherever you like. You announced yesterday, at father's, that there's no God." Alyosha looked searchingly at his brother.

"I said that yesterday at dinner on purpose, to tease you, and I saw your eyes light up. But I've got no objection to discussing it with you now, and I say that quite seriously. I want us to be friends, Alyosha, because I have no friends, and I want to try having one. Well, just imagine, maybe I accept God too," Ivan laughed; "that's a surprise for you, isn't it?"
"Yes, of course, if you're not joking now."

"Joking? I was told at the elder's yesterday that I was joking. You know, dear boy, there was an old sinner back in the eighteenth century who declared that if God didn't exist, He'd have to be invented. _S'il n'existait pas Dieu, il faudrait l'inventer._ And man has, in fact, invented God. And what's strange, what would truly be marvelous, isn't that God should actually exist—the marvel is that such an idea, the idea of the necessity of God, could ever occur to such a savage, vicious beast as man. So holy is it, so moving, so wise, and such credit does it do to mankind. As for me, I made up my mind long ago not to trouble over whether man created God or God created man. And I won't run through all the axioms Russian boys lay down on that subject, all borrowed from European hypotheses—because what's a hypothesis there is treated as an axiom by the Russian boy, and not only by the boys but by their teachers too, since our Russian professors are often just the same boys themselves, grown up. So I'll skip all the hypotheses. What are we actually driving at here? I'm trying to explain, as quickly as I can, my essential nature—what sort of man I am, what I believe, what I hope for—that's it, isn't it? And so I tell you, I accept God, plainly and simply. But note this: if God exists, and if He really did create the world, then, as we all know, He created it according to Euclidean geometry, and the human mind with the concept of only three dimensions in space. And yet there have been, and still are, geometers and philosophers—some of them among the most distinguished—who wonder whether the whole universe, or more broadly speaking, the whole of existence, was really created only according to Euclid's geometry; they even dare to imagine that two parallel lines, which by Euclid's rules can never meet on earth, might meet somewhere out in infinity. I've come to the conclusion that since I can't even understand that much, I certainly can't expect to understand anything about God. I admit humbly that I lack the capacity to settle such questions; I have a Euclidean, earthly mind, so how could I possibly solve problems that don't belong to this world at all? And my advice to you is never to think about it either, my dear Alyosha, especially about God, about whether He exists or not. All such questions are simply unsuited to a mind built around only three dimensions. And so I accept God, and gladly, and what's more, I accept His wisdom, His purpose, which lie utterly beyond our grasp; I believe in some underlying order, some meaning to life; I believe in the eternal harmony they say we'll all be blended into one day. I believe in the Word toward which the universe is striving, the Word that was itself 'with God,' and that is itself God, and so on, and so on, into infinity. There are all sorts of phrases for it. I seem to be on the right track, don't I? And yet, would you believe it, in the end I don't accept this world of God's—and even though I know it exists, I don't accept it at all. It's not that I reject God, you understand, it's the world He created that I don't, and can't, accept. Let me put it plainly. I believe, like a child, that suffering will be healed, made up for, that all the humiliating absurdity of human contradictions will vanish like some pitiful mirage, like the wretched invention of man's feeble, infinitely small Euclidean mind, that in the world's final act, at the moment of eternal harmony, something so precious will happen that it will be enough for every heart, enough to soothe every grievance, to atone for every crime humanity has ever committed, for all the blood they've spilled; that it will make it possible not merely to forgive but to justify everything that has ever happened to men—but even if all that comes to pass, I still don't accept it. I won't accept it. Even if the parallel lines meet and I see it with my own eyes, I'll see it and say they've met, but I still won't accept it. That's what lies at the root of me, Alyosha; that's my creed. I'm entirely serious about what I'm saying. I began our conversation as stupidly as I possibly could, on purpose, but it's led straight to my confession, because that's really all you wanted. You didn't want to hear about God—you wanted to know what the brother you love actually lives by. And now I've told you."
Ivan wrapped up his long tirade with a striking, unexpected show of feeling.
"And why did you begin 'as stupidly as you could'?" Alyosha asked, gazing dreamily at him.

"For one thing, for the sake of being Russian. Russian conversations on subjects like this are always carried on with unbelievable stupidity. And second, the more stupid one is, the closer one gets to reality. Stupidity is blunt and artless, while intelligence squirms and hides itself away. Intelligence is a swindler, but stupidity is honest and straightforward. I've steered the conversation toward my own despair, and the more stupidly I've laid it out, the better for me."
"You'll explain why you don't accept the world?" Alyosha said.

"Of course I will, it's no secret, it's exactly what I've been building up to. Dear little brother, I don't want to corrupt you, or shake you loose from your foundation—maybe I want you to heal me instead." Ivan suddenly smiled, quite like a gentle little child. Alyosha had never seen a smile like that on his face before.

title: IV. Rebellion
paragraphs: "I have to make you a confession," Ivan began. "I've never been able to understand how one is supposed to love one's neighbor. It's precisely one's neighbors, to my mind, that are impossible to love—though one might manage to love people from a distance. I once read somewhere about a saint, John the Merciful, that when a hungry, frozen beggar came to him, he took the man into his own bed, held him in his arms, and began breathing into his mouth, which was foul and putrid from some horrible disease. I'm convinced he did that out of 'self-laceration,' out of the self-laceration of falseness, for the sake of a charity imposed as duty, as a penance laid on himself. For anyone to love another person, that person has to stay hidden, because the moment he shows his face, the love vanishes."

"Father Zosima has said something like that more than once," Alyosha observed. "He too said that a man's face often keeps people who aren't practiced in love from loving him. And yet there's a great deal of love in mankind, love that's almost Christlike. I know that myself, Ivan."

"Well, I know nothing of it so far, and I can't understand it, and the vast bulk of mankind is right there with me. The question is whether that's down to men's bad qualities or whether it's simply built into their nature. To my mind, Christlike love for one's fellow man is a miracle impossible here on earth. He was God. We are not gods. Suppose, for instance, that I suffer intensely. No one else can ever know exactly how much I suffer, because he is someone else, not me. And what's more, a man is rarely willing to admit another person's suffering, as though it were some kind of distinction. Why won't he admit it, do you think? Because I smell unpleasant, because I've got a stupid face, because I once stepped on his foot. Besides, there's suffering and there's suffering; degrading, humiliating suffering, the kind that humbles me—hunger, say—my benefactor might allow for that; but when you get to a higher kind of suffering—suffering for an idea, say—he'll rarely admit that at all, maybe because my face doesn't match what he imagines a man suffering for an idea ought to look like. And so he strips me of his favor on the spot, and not out of any real malice. Beggars, especially genteel ones, ought never to show themselves in person, but should beg for charity through the newspapers instead. One can love one's neighbors in the abstract, or even from a distance, but up close it's almost impossible. If it were like on stage, in the ballet, where beggars come on wearing silk rags and tattered lace, begging for alms in graceful little dances, then one might enjoy watching them. But even then we wouldn't really love them. But enough of that. I only wanted to show you my point of view. I meant to talk about the suffering of humanity in general, but we'd better limit ourselves to the suffering of children. That cuts my argument down to a tenth of its scope, but we'd better stick to children, even though it weakens my case. But, first, children can be loved even up close, even when they're dirty, even when they're ugly—though I don't think children are ever really ugly. The second reason I won't talk about grown-ups is that, besides being repulsive and unworthy of love, they've got a kind of compensation—they've eaten the apple and know good and evil, they've become 'like gods.' And they go on eating it still. But children haven't eaten anything, and so far they're innocent. Do you love children, Alyosha? I know you do, and you'll understand why I'd rather talk about them. If they too suffer horribly on this earth, it must be for their fathers' sins, they must be punished on their fathers' behalf, for the fathers who ate the apple—but that kind of reasoning belongs to another world, and it's incomprehensible to the human heart here on earth. The innocent shouldn't suffer for someone else's sins, and especially not innocents like these! You might be surprised at me, Alyosha, but I'm terribly fond of children too. And notice this: cruel people, violent people, rapacious people, Karamazovs even, are often very fond of children. Children, while they're still quite small—up to seven, say—are so remote from grown-ups; they're practically a different species, as it were. I knew a criminal in prison who had, over the course of his career as a burglar, murdered whole families, children included. But once he was locked up, he developed a strange fondness for them. He spent all his time at his window watching the children play in the prison yard. He trained one little boy to come up to his window and became great friends with him.... You don't know why I'm telling you all this, Alyosha? My head aches, and I'm sad."
"You have a strange way of talking," Alyosha observed uneasily, "as if you weren't quite yourself."

"By the way, a Bulgarian I met recently in Moscow," Ivan went on, as though he hadn't heard his brother's remark, "told me about the crimes the Turks and Circassians have been committing all over Bulgaria, out of fear of a general uprising of the Slavs. They burn villages, they murder, they violate women and children, they nail their prisoners' ears to the fences and leave them there until morning, and in the morning they hang them—all sorts of things you couldn't even imagine. People talk sometimes about 'bestial' cruelty, but that's a great injustice, an insult to the beasts; no animal could ever be as cruel as a man, so artistically cruel. A tiger only tears and gnaws, that's all it knows how to do. It would never think of nailing people's ears to anything, even if it could. Those Turks took real pleasure in torturing children too—cutting an unborn child out of its mother's womb, tossing babies into the air and catching them on the points of their bayonets, right in front of their mothers' eyes. Doing it in front of the mothers was what gave the whole thing its flavor. Here's another scene I found particularly striking. Picture a trembling mother holding her baby, surrounded by a ring of Turkish soldiers. They've dreamed up a little diversion: they pet the baby, they laugh to make it laugh. It works, the baby laughs. At that moment a Turk points a pistol four inches from the baby's face. The baby laughs with delight, reaches its little hands toward the pistol, and he pulls the trigger right in the baby's face and blows its brains out. Artistic, wasn't it? By the way, they say Turks are particularly fond of sweets."
"Brother, what are you getting at?" Alyosha asked.
"I think that if the devil doesn't exist, and man has invented him, then man has invented him in his own image and likeness."
"Just as he did with God, then?" Alyosha observed.

"'Tis wonderful how you can turn words, as Polonius says in Hamlet," Ivan laughed. "You're turning my own words against me. Well, I'm glad. Yours must be a fine God, if man created Him in his own image and likeness. You just asked what I was getting at. You see, I have a fondness for collecting certain facts—I even copy anecdotes of a certain kind out of newspapers and books, and would you believe, I've already put together quite a collection. The Turks, of course, are part of it, but they're foreigners. I've got homegrown specimens that are even better than the Turks. You know we favor beating here—rods and whips, that's our national tradition. Nailing ears is unthinkable for us, since we are, after all, Europeans. But the rod and the whip we've always had with us, and no one can take them away. Abroad these days they've mostly given up beating. Manners have grown more humane, or laws have been passed, so they no longer dare flog people. But they make up for it in another way, just as national in its own place as ours is here. So national, in fact, that it would be nearly impossible for us—though I think we're being inoculated with it, now that the religious movement has started up among our aristocracy. I have a charming pamphlet, translated from the French, describing the execution, quite recently, five years ago, of a murderer named Richard—a young man, I believe, twenty-three, who repented and converted to the Christian faith right there on the scaffold. This Richard was an illegitimate child, handed over by his parents at the age of six to some shepherds in the Swiss mountains. They raised him to work for them. He grew up among them like a little wild animal. The shepherds taught him nothing, barely fed or clothed him, and sent him out at seven to herd sheep in the cold and wet, and not one of them hesitated or felt a shred of scruple about treating him that way. Quite the opposite—they thought they had every right to, since Richard had been handed over to them like a piece of property, and they didn't even see the need to feed him. Richard himself describes how, during those years, like the Prodigal Son in the Gospel, he longed to eat the mash they fed the pigs, which were being fattened for sale. But they wouldn't even give him that, and beat him whenever he stole it from the pigs. That's how he spent his entire childhood and youth, until he grew up and was strong enough to run off and become a thief. This savage began earning his living as a day laborer in Geneva. He drank away his wages, lived like an animal, and ended up killing and robbing an old man. He was caught, tried, and sentenced to death. They're not sentimentalists over there. And in prison he was immediately surrounded by pastors, members of Christian brotherhoods, philanthropic ladies, and the like. They taught him to read and write in prison, expounded the Gospel to him. They exhorted him, worked on him, drummed at him without letup, until at last he solemnly confessed his crime. He was converted. He wrote to the court himself that he was a monster, but that in the end God had granted him light and shown him grace. All of Geneva was in an uproar over him—all philanthropic, religious Geneva. All the aristocratic, well-bred society of the town rushed to the prison, kissed Richard, embraced him: 'You are our brother, you have found grace.' And all Richard does is weep with emotion: 'Yes, I've found grace! All through my youth and childhood I was glad to get pigs' food, but now even I have found grace. I am dying in the Lord.' 'Yes, Richard, die in the Lord; you shed blood, and you must die. It's not your fault you didn't know the Lord, back when you coveted the pigs' food and were beaten for stealing it—which was very wrong of you, mind, since stealing is forbidden—but you shed blood, and you must die.' And on the last day, Richard, utterly limp, does nothing but weep and repeat over and over: 'This is the happiest day of my life. I am going to the Lord.' 'Yes,' cry the pastors and the judges and the philanthropic ladies. 'This is the happiest day of your life, for you are going to the Lord!' They all walk or ride in procession to the scaffold, behind the prison cart. At the scaffold they call out to Richard: 'Die, brother, die in the Lord, for even you have found grace!' And so, covered in his brothers' kisses, Richard is dragged up onto the scaffold and led to the guillotine. And they chop off his head in the most brotherly fashion, because he had found grace. Yes, that's very telling. That pamphlet was translated into Russian by some Russian philanthropists of aristocratic rank with evangelical leanings, and it's been distributed free of charge, for the enlightenment of the people. The Richard case is interesting because it's so national in its own way. Even though it strikes us as absurd to cut off a man's head just because he's become our brother and found grace, we've got our own specialty, which is arguably even worse. Our historical pastime is inflicting pain, straight up, for the sheer satisfaction of it. There are lines in Nekrasov describing a peasant lashing a horse across the eyes, 'across its meek eyes'—everyone must have seen it. It's peculiarly Russian. He describes a feeble little nag that's buckled under too heavy a load and can't move. The peasant beats it, beats it savagely, beats it at last without even knowing what he's doing, drunk on cruelty, thrashing it over and over without mercy. 'However weak you are, you'll pull it, even if it kills you.' The nag strains, and then he starts lashing the poor defenseless creature across its weeping, its 'meek eyes.' The frantic animal tugs and hauls the load, trembling all over, gasping for breath, lurching sideways in some unnatural, spasmodic motion—it's dreadful, in Nekrasov. But that's only a horse, and God gave us horses to be beaten. Or so the Tatars taught us, and left us the knout as a keepsake. But men can be beaten too. A well-educated, cultured gentleman and his wife once beat their own child with a birch rod—a girl of seven. I have the exact account of it. The father was pleased that the birch had plenty of twigs on it. 'It stings more,' he said, and set about stinging his daughter. I know for a fact there are people who, with every blow, work themselves into a kind of sensual pleasure, literal sensuality, that grows and grows with every blow they land. They beat the child for a minute, five minutes, ten minutes, harder and more savagely as they go. The child screams. Eventually the child can't scream anymore, just gasps, 'Daddy! Daddy!' By some diabolical, unseemly stroke of chance, the case ended up in court. A lawyer is hired. Russians have long called a defense lawyer 'a conscience for hire.' The lawyer protests in his client's defense: 'It's such a simple matter,' he says, 'an everyday domestic occurrence. A father disciplines his child. To our shame, it's ended up in court.' The jury, won over, returns a favorable verdict. The public roars with delight that the torturer has been acquitted. Ah, what a pity I wasn't there! I'd have proposed taking up a collection in his honor! Charming pictures.

"But I've got even better ones about children. I've collected a great, great deal about Russian children, Alyosha. There was a little girl of five whose own father and mother hated her—'most respectable, worthy people, well-educated and well-bred.' You see, I have to say it again: it's a peculiar trait in a lot of people, this love of torturing children, children specifically. Toward every other kind of person, these same torturers behave gently, generously even, like proper cultivated, humane Europeans; but they're very fond of tormenting children—fond, even, of the children themselves, in that particular sense. It's precisely the child's helplessness that tempts the tormentor, precisely the angelic trust of a child who has no refuge and no appeal, that sets his vile blood boiling. In every man, of course, there's a demon hidden away—the demon of rage, the demon of lustful heat at the screams of a tortured victim, the demon of lawlessness let off its chain, the demon of the diseases that come with vice—gout, kidney trouble, and so on.

"This poor five-year-old was subjected to every torture imaginable by those cultivated parents. They beat her, thrashed her, kicked her for no reason at all until her whole body was one bruise. Then they moved on to still finer refinements of cruelty—locked her up all night, in the cold and frost, in an outhouse, and because she didn't ask to be let out at night (as if a five-year-old, sunk in her angelic, deep sleep, could somehow be trained to wake up and ask), they smeared her face with excrement and forced it into her mouth—and it was her mother, her own mother, who did this. And that mother could sleep at night, hearing the poor child's groans! Can you understand why a small creature, who can't even grasp what's being done to her, would beat her aching little chest with her tiny fist, alone in the dark and the cold, and weep her meek, uncomplaining tears to 'dear, kind God' to protect her? Do you understand that, my friend, my brother, you pious, humble little novice? Do you understand why this outrage has to happen, and is allowed to happen? Without it, I'm told, man couldn't have existed on earth at all, because he couldn't have known good and evil. Why should he need to know that devilish good and evil, when it costs so much? Why, the entire world of knowledge isn't worth that one child's prayer to 'dear, kind God'! I say nothing about the sufferings of grown-ups—they ate the apple, damn them, and the devil take the lot of them! But these little ones! I'm making you suffer, Alyosha, you're not yourself. I'll stop if you want."
"Never mind. I want to suffer too," Alyosha murmured.

"One picture, just one more, because it's so striking, so telling, and I only just read it in some collection of Russian antiquities—I've forgotten the title, I must look it up. This was in the darkest days of serfdom, at the beginning of the century—and long live the Liberator of the People! In those days there was a general, well connected among the aristocracy, the owner of vast estates, one of those men—somewhat exceptional, I believe, even for that time—who, retiring from service into a life of leisure, become convinced they've earned absolute power over the lives of their subjects. There were men like that back then. So our general, settled on his estate of two thousand souls, lives in splendor, lording it over his poor neighbors as though they were dependents put on earth to amuse him. He keeps kennels with hundreds of hounds and nearly a hundred dog-boys—all mounted, all in uniform. One day a serf boy, a small child of eight, threw a stone while playing and hurt the paw of the general's favorite hound. 'Why is my favorite dog limping?' He's told that the boy threw a stone and hurt the dog's paw. 'So it was you.' The general looks the child up and down. 'Take him.' The boy is taken—taken from his mother and locked up overnight. Early the next morning the general rides out on horseback with the hounds, his dependents, his dog-boys and huntsmen, all mounted around him in full hunting dress. The household servants are summoned to witness, for their own edification, and standing in front of them all is the child's mother. The boy is brought out from the lockup. It's a gloomy, cold, foggy autumn day, a perfect day for a hunt. The general orders the child stripped; the boy is stripped bare. He shivers, numb with terror, not even daring to cry.... 'Make him run,' the general commands. 'Run! Run!' the dog-boys shout. The boy runs.... 'Sic him!' the general bellows, and he sets the entire pack of hounds on the child. The hounds catch him and tear him to pieces before his mother's eyes!... I believe the general was later declared unfit to manage his own estates. Well—what did he deserve? To be shot? Shot, for the satisfaction of our moral feelings? Speak, Alyosha!"
"To be shot," Alyosha murmured, lifting his eyes to Ivan with a pale, twisted smile.
"Bravo!" Ivan cried, delighted. "If even you say so.... What a fine monk you are! So there's a little devil sitting in your heart too, Alyosha Karamazov!"
"What I said was absurd, but—"

"That's exactly the point, that 'but'!" Ivan cried. "Let me tell you, novice, the absurd is one of the most necessary things on earth. The world rests on absurdities, and maybe nothing would ever have happened in it without them. We know what we know!"
"What do you know?"

"I understand nothing," Ivan went on, as though in delirium. "I don't want to understand anything anymore. I want to stick to the fact. I made up my mind long ago not to understand. If I try to understand anything, I'll betray the fact, and I've resolved to stick to the fact."
"Why are you testing me like this?" Alyosha cried, suddenly distressed. "Will you finally say what you mean?"
"Of course I will; that's exactly what I've been building up to. You're dear to me, I don't want to let you go, and I won't hand you over to your Zosima."
Ivan fell silent for a moment, and his face suddenly turned very sad.

"Listen! I only took the case of children to make my argument clearer. I'll say nothing about the rest of humanity's tears, which soak the earth from its crust to its core. I've deliberately narrowed my subject. I'm a bug, and I admit, in all humility, that I can't understand why the world is arranged the way it is. Men are to blame for it themselves, I suppose; they were given paradise, they wanted freedom, and they stole fire from heaven knowing perfectly well they'd become unhappy for it, so there's no need to pity them. With my pitiful, earthbound, Euclidean understanding, all I know is that there's suffering, and that no one is guilty; that cause follows effect, simply and directly; that everything flows and finds its own level—but that's just Euclidean nonsense, I know that much, and I can't bring myself to live by it! What good does it do me that no one is guilty and that cause follows effect simply and directly, and that I understand that perfectly well? I need justice, or I'll destroy myself. And not justice somewhere off in infinite time and space, but here, on earth, justice I could see with my own eyes. I've believed in it. I want to see it for myself, and if I'm already dead by then, let me rise again, because if it all happens without me, it'll be too unfair. Surely I haven't suffered simply so that I, my crimes and my sufferings, could go to fertilize the soil for someone else's future harmony. I want to see, with my own eyes, the doe lie down with the lion, and the murdered man rise up and embrace his murderer. I want to be there when everyone suddenly understands what it was all for. All the religions of the world are built on that longing, and I am a believer. But then there are the children, and what am I supposed to do about them? That's a question I can't answer. For the hundredth time, I repeat, there are countless questions, but I've only taken up the children, because in their case, what I mean is so unanswerably clear. Listen! If everyone has to suffer to pay for the eternal harmony, what do children have to do with it, tell me, please? It's utterly incomprehensible why they should have to suffer, why they should have to pay for that harmony. Why should they too have to serve as raw material to enrich the soil for some future harmony? I understand solidarity in sin among adults. I understand solidarity in punishment too. But there can be no such solidarity with children. And if it's really true that they have to share responsibility for all their fathers' crimes, then that kind of truth doesn't belong to this world, and it's beyond my comprehension. Some wit might say, perhaps, that the child would have grown up and sinned eventually anyway, but you see, he didn't grow up—he was torn to pieces by dogs at the age of eight. Oh, Alyosha, I'm not blaspheming! I understand, of course, what an upheaval of the whole universe it will be, when everything in heaven and on earth blends into one great hymn of praise, and everything that lives and has ever lived cries out: 'Thou art just, O Lord, for Thy ways are revealed.' When the mother embraces the fiend who threw her child to the dogs, and all three of them cry out through their tears, 'Thou art just, O Lord!'—then, of course, the crown of all knowledge will be reached, and everything will be made clear. But what stops me cold, right here, is that I can't accept that harmony. And while I'm still on this earth, I hurry to take my own precautions. You see, Alyosha, it may very well happen that if I live to see that moment, or rise again to witness it, I too might cry out with all the rest, watching the mother embrace her child's torturer: 'Thou art just, O Lord!'—but I don't want to cry that out then. While there's still time, I hasten to protect myself now, and so I renounce that higher harmony altogether. It isn't worth the tears of that one tortured child who beat her aching chest with her little fist and prayed in her filthy outhouse, with her unavenged tears, to 'dear, kind God'! It isn't worth it, because those tears remain unatoned for. They have to be atoned for, or there can be no harmony at all. But how? How could you possibly atone for them? Is it even possible? By avenging them? But what do I care about avenging them? What do I care about a hell for the oppressors? What good could hell possibly do, once those children have already been tortured? And what becomes of harmony, if there's a hell? I want to forgive. I want to embrace. I don't want any more suffering. And if the sufferings of children are meant to swell the total sum of suffering needed to purchase the truth, then I protest that the truth isn't worth such a price. I don't want the mother to embrace the man who threw her son to the dogs! She has no right to forgive him! Let her forgive him for herself, if she wants to, let her forgive the torturer for the immeasurable suffering inflicted on her as a mother. But she has no right to forgive him the suffering of her tortured child; she dare not forgive the torturer that, even if the child himself were to forgive him! And if that's so, if they dare not forgive, then what becomes of harmony? Is there anyone anywhere in the whole world who would have the right to forgive, and who actually could forgive? I don't want harmony. Out of love for humanity, I don't want it. I would rather be left with suffering that goes unavenged. I would rather stay with my unavenged suffering and my unsatisfied indignation, even if I turn out to be wrong. Besides, the price being asked for harmony is too high; it's beyond our means to pay that much just to get in. And so I hurry to hand back my entrance ticket, and if I'm an honest man, I'm bound to hand it back as soon as I possibly can. And that's exactly what I'm doing. It's not God I don't accept, Alyosha—it's just that I most respectfully return Him the ticket."
"That's rebellion," Alyosha murmured, looking down.

"Rebellion? I'm sorry you'd call it that," Ivan said earnestly. "One can hardly live in a state of rebellion, and I want to live. Tell me yourself, I'm putting it to you directly—answer me. Imagine that you're constructing the fabric of human destiny, with the ultimate goal of making people happy in the end, giving them peace and rest at last—but that to do it, it was essential, unavoidable, to torture just one tiny creature to death—that baby beating its chest with its little fist, say—and to build that whole edifice on her unavenged tears—would you agree to be the architect, on those terms? Tell me, and tell the truth."
"No, I wouldn't agree," Alyosha said softly.

"And can you accept the idea that the people you're building it for would actually agree to accept their happiness on the foundation of one small victim's unatoned-for blood? And having accepted it, remain happy forever after?"

"No, I can't accept that. Brother," Alyosha said suddenly, his eyes flashing, "you just asked whether there's anyone in the whole world who has the right to forgive, and who could forgive. But there is such a Being, and He can forgive everything, everyone, for everything, because He gave His own innocent blood for all of it, for everyone. You've forgotten Him, and it's on Him that the whole edifice is built, and it's to Him that they cry out, 'Thou art just, O Lord, for Thy ways are revealed!'"

"Ah! The One without sin, and His blood! No, I haven't forgotten Him—quite the opposite, I've been wondering this whole time why you hadn't brought Him up sooner, since usually every argument on your side puts Him front and center. Do you know, Alyosha—don't laugh!—I composed a poem about a year ago. If you can spare me another ten minutes, I'll tell it to you."
"You wrote a poem?"

"Oh, no, I didn't write it down," Ivan laughed, "and I've never written two lines of verse in my life. But I made up this poem in prose, and I remember it. I got carried away composing it. You'll be my first reader—that is, my first listener. Why should an author pass up even one listener?" Ivan smiled. "Shall I tell it to you?"
"I'm listening," said Alyosha.
"My poem is called 'The Grand Inquisitor'; it's a ridiculous thing, but I want to tell it to you."

title: V. The Grand Inquisitor
paragraphs: "Even this needs a preface—a literary one, I mean," Ivan laughed, "and I'm not much good at writing one. You see, my story takes place in the sixteenth century, and back then, as you probably learned in school, it was common in poetry to bring the powers of heaven down to earth. Never mind Dante—in France, clerks as well as monastery monks used to put on regular performances in which the Madonna, the saints, the angels, Christ, even God Himself, were brought onto the stage. In those days it was all done with perfect innocence. In Victor Hugo's Notre-Dame de Paris, an edifying, free spectacle was staged for the people at the Hôtel de Ville in Paris, during the reign of Louis XI, to celebrate the birth of the dauphin. It was called Le bon jugement de la très sainte et gracieuse Vierge Marie, and the Virgin herself appears on stage and delivers her bon jugement. Similar plays, mostly drawn from the Old Testament, were occasionally performed in Moscow too, right up through the reign of Peter the Great. But besides actual plays, there were all sorts of legends and ballads scattered across the world in which saints and angels and every power of Heaven took part whenever the story called for them. In our monasteries, the monks busied themselves translating, copying, even composing poems of that kind—even under the Tatars. There's one, for instance—from the Greek, of course—called The Wanderings of Our Lady Through Hell, with descriptions as bold as Dante's. Our Lady visits hell, and the Archangel Michael guides her through the torments. She sees the sinners and their punishments. Among them she notices one particularly striking group of sinners sunk in a burning lake; some of them sink so deep they can never swim back up, and 'these, God forgets'—a phrase of extraordinary depth and force. And so Our Lady, shaken and weeping, falls down before the throne of God and begs mercy for everyone in hell—for everyone she saw there, without exception. Her exchange with God is fascinating. She pleads, she won't let up, and when God points to the hands and feet of her Son, nailed to the Cross, and asks, 'How can I forgive His tormentors?', she calls on all the saints, all the martyrs, all the angels and archangels to fall down beside her and pray for mercy on everyone, without distinction. It ends with her winning a yearly reprieve from suffering, from Good Friday to Trinity Day, and the sinners in hell immediately cry out in gratitude, chanting: 'Thou art just, O Lord, in this judgment.' Well, my poem would have been something along those lines, if it had appeared back then. He appears on the scene in my poem, but He says nothing—He simply appears, and passes on. Fifteen centuries have gone by since He promised to come in His glory, fifteen centuries since His prophet wrote, 'Behold, I come quickly'; 'of that day and that hour knoweth no man, neither the Son, but the Father,' as He Himself foretold while on earth. But humanity still waits for Him with the same faith, the same love. Oh, with even greater faith, since it's been fifteen centuries since man stopped seeing signs from heaven."
No signs from heaven come today / To back up what the heart doth say.

"There was nothing left but faith in what the heart says. It's true, there were plenty of miracles in those days. There were saints who performed miraculous cures; some holy people, according to their biographies, were visited by the Queen of Heaven herself. But the devil never sleeps, and doubts about the truth of these miracles had already started creeping in among men. And right around then a terrifying new heresy sprang up in northern Germany. 'A huge star, like a torch'—meaning a church—'fell upon the sources of the waters, and they became bitter.' These heretics began blasphemously denying miracles outright. But those who stayed faithful believed all the more fervently for it. Humanity's tears rose up to Him as before, waiting for His coming, loving Him, hoping in Him, yearning to suffer and die for Him just as before. And after so many centuries of praying with faith and fervor, 'O Lord our God, hasten Thy coming,' after calling on Him for so many ages, He, in His infinite mercy, chose to come down among His servants once more. Before that day, He had come down before—He'd visited certain holy men, martyrs and hermits, as their lives record. Among us, Tyutchev, with absolute faith in the truth of what he wrote, testified that"
Bearing the Cross, in servant's dress, Weary and worn, the Heavenly King Our mother Russia came to bless, And through our land went wandering.
"And that certainly was so, I assure you.

"And behold, He chose to appear, if only for a moment, to His people—the tortured, suffering people, sunk in wickedness, yet loving Him like children. My story is set in Spain, in Seville, at the most terrible height of the Inquisition, when fires were lit every day to the glory of God, and 'in a splendid auto-da-fé the wicked heretics were burned.' Oh, of course this isn't the coming He promised, the one where He will appear at the end of time in the full glory of heaven, sudden 'as lightning flashing from east to west.' No, He came to visit His children only for a moment, right there where the flames were crackling around the heretics. In His infinite mercy He walked once more among men in that same human form in which He had walked among them for three years, fifteen centuries before. He came down onto the 'hot pavements' of that southern town, where only the day before, almost a hundred heretics had been burned, ad majorem gloriam Dei, by the cardinal, the Grand Inquisitor, in a magnificent auto-da-fé, before the king, the court, the knights, the cardinals, the loveliest ladies of the court, and the entire population of Seville."

"He came quietly, unnoticed, and yet, strange to say, everyone recognized Him. This might be one of the best parts of the poem—I mean, why they recognized Him. The people are irresistibly drawn to Him, they crowd around Him, gather close, follow Him. He moves silently among them with a gentle smile of infinite compassion. The sun of love burns in His heart, light and power pour from His eyes, and their radiance, falling on the people, stirs their hearts with an answering love. He holds out His hands to them, blesses them, and a healing power flows from His touch, even just from touching His clothes. An old man in the crowd, blind since childhood, cries out, 'O Lord, heal me, and I shall see Thee!' and something like scales fall from his eyes, and the blind man sees Him. The crowd weeps and kisses the earth beneath His feet. Children throw flowers before Him, sing, cry out hosanna. 'It is He—it is He!' they all repeat. 'It must be Him, it can be no one else!' He stops at the steps of Seville Cathedral just as weeping mourners are carrying in a small open white coffin. Inside lies a child of seven, the only daughter of a prominent citizen. The dead child lies buried in flowers. 'He will raise your child,' the crowd shouts to the weeping mother. The priest, coming out to meet the coffin, looks baffled and frowns, but the dead child's mother throws herself at His feet with a wail. 'If it is truly Thou, raise my child!' she cries, stretching her hands toward Him. The procession stops, the coffin is set down on the steps at His feet. He looks on with compassion, and His lips softly say once more: 'Maiden, arise.' And the maiden rises. The little girl sits up in the coffin and looks around, smiling with wide, wondering eyes, still holding the bunch of white roses they'd placed in her hand."

"There are cries, sobs, confusion among the crowd, and at that very moment the cardinal himself, the Grand Inquisitor, passes by the cathedral. He is an old man, almost ninety, tall and upright, with a withered face and sunken eyes in which a gleam of light still lingers. He isn't wearing his magnificent cardinal's robes, as he was the day before, when he was burning the enemies of the Roman Church—at this moment he wears his coarse, old monk's cassock. Following him, at some distance, come his grim assistants and slaves and the 'holy guard.' He stops at the sight of the crowd and watches from a distance. He sees everything; he sees them set the coffin down at His feet, sees the child rise, and his face darkens. He knits his thick gray brows, and his eyes flash with a sinister fire. He points a finger and orders the guards to seize Him. And such is his power, so completely have the people been cowed into trembling obedience to him, that the crowd immediately parts for the guards, and in dead silence they lay hands on Him and lead Him away. The crowd instantly bows to the ground, as one man, before the old Inquisitor. He blesses the people in silence and moves on. The guards lead their prisoner to the cramped, gloomy, vaulted prison inside the ancient palace of the Holy Inquisition, and lock Him in. The day passes, followed by the dark, scorching, 'breathless' night of Seville. The air 'smells of laurel and lemon.' In the pitch darkness, the iron door of the prison suddenly opens, and the Grand Inquisitor himself walks in, carrying a light. He is alone; the door closes behind him at once. He stands in the doorway and for a minute or two gazes into His face. At last he walks up slowly, sets the light down on the table, and speaks."

"'Is it Thou? Thou?' But getting no answer, he adds at once, 'Don't answer, stay silent. What could You possibly say, anyway? I already know full well what You would say. And You have no right to add a single word to what You said long ago. Then why have You come to get in our way? For You have come to get in our way, and You know it perfectly well. But do You know what will happen tomorrow? I don't know who You are, and I don't care to know whether it's really You, or only something in Your likeness, but tomorrow I will condemn You and burn You at the stake as the worst of heretics. And the very people who kissed Your feet today will, at the first sign from me, rush to pile the embers of Your fire even higher. Do You know that? Yes, perhaps You do know it,' he added, with a thoughtful, searching look, never once taking his eyes off the Prisoner."

"I don't quite follow, Ivan. What does it all mean?" Alyosha, who had been listening in silence, asked with a smile. "Is it just some wild fantasy, or is the old man making some kind of mistake—some impossible case of mistaken identity?"

"Take it as the last one, if you like," Ivan said, laughing, "if you're so corrupted by modern realism that you can't stomach anything fantastical. If you'd rather it be a case of mistaken identity, let it be that. It's true," he went on, laughing, "the old man was ninety, and he might well have gone half-mad clinging to his fixed idea. He might have simply been struck by the Prisoner's appearance. It might, in fact, be nothing more than the ravings of a ninety-year-old, overwrought by yesterday's auto-da-fé of a hundred heretics. But does it really matter to us whether it was mistaken identity or pure fantasy? All that matters is that the old man finally speaks his mind, speaks openly about what he's kept silent for ninety years."
"And the Prisoner is silent too? He just looks at him and doesn't say a word?"

"That's unavoidable, in any version of the story," Ivan laughed again. "The old man has already told Him He has no right to add anything to what He said long ago. You might say that's the most fundamental feature of Roman Catholicism—in my opinion, at least. 'Everything has been handed over by You to the Pope,' they say, 'and so everything now rests in the Pope's hands, and there's no need for You to come back at all. For now, at least, You mustn't interfere.' That's how they talk, and how they write too—the Jesuits, anyway. I've read it myself in the works of their theologians. 'Do You have the right to reveal to us even one of the mysteries of that world You came from?' my old man asks Him, and then answers the question for Him. 'No, You do not; because that would mean adding to what was said long ago, and would strip men of the freedom You exalted so highly while You walked the earth. Anything You reveal now, anything new, will encroach on men's freedom of belief, because it will present itself as a miracle, and the freedom of their faith was dearer to You than anything else, back then, fifteen hundred years ago. Didn't You say, often enough, in those days, "I will make you free"? But now You've seen these "free" men,' the old man adds suddenly, with a pensive smile. 'Yes, we've paid a heavy price for it,' he goes on, looking sternly at Him, 'but at last we've finished that work, in Your name. For fifteen centuries we have wrestled with Your freedom, but now it is finished, over for good. You don't believe it's over for good? You look at me so meekly, and don't even deign to be angry with me. But let me tell You: right now, today, people are more convinced than ever that they possess complete freedom, and yet they've brought that very freedom to us and laid it humbly at our feet. And that has been our doing. Is this what You wanted? Is this the freedom You meant?'"
"I don't follow again," Alyosha broke in. "Is he being ironic? Is he joking?"

"Not in the least! He claims it as an achievement, for himself and his Church, that at last they've conquered freedom, and done so in order to make men happy. 'For now'—he's talking about the Inquisition, of course—'for the first time, it's become possible to think about the happiness of men. Man was created a rebel; and how can rebels be happy?' he says to Him. 'You were warned. You had no shortage of admonitions and warnings, but You wouldn't heed them; You rejected the only way men could ever be made happy. But fortunately, on Your way out, You passed the work on to us. You promised it, You established it by Your own word, You gave us the right to bind and to loose, and now, of course, You can't possibly think of taking that back. So why have You come to get in our way now?'"
"And what does he mean by 'no shortage of admonitions and warnings'?" Alyosha asked.
"Why, that's the heart of what the old man has to say.

"'The wise and dread spirit, the spirit of self-destruction and non-existence,' the old man goes on, 'the great spirit spoke with You in the wilderness, and we're told in the books that he "tempted" You. Is that so? And could anything truer ever have been said than what he revealed to You in those three questions, which You rejected, and which the books call "the temptation"? And yet, if there has ever been a truly stupendous miracle on this earth, it happened that day, the day of the three temptations. The very posing of those three questions was itself the miracle. Suppose, just for the sake of argument, that those three questions from the dread spirit had vanished entirely from the books, and that we had to reconstruct them, invent them fresh, and to do so gathered together every wise man on earth—rulers, high priests, scholars, philosophers, poets—and set them the task of inventing three questions that would not only fit the occasion, but would express, in three words, three human phrases, the entire future history of the world and of humanity—do You believe that all the combined wisdom of the earth could have come up with anything to match, in depth and force, the three questions actually put to You then, by the wise and mighty spirit in the wilderness? From those three questions alone, from the sheer miracle of how they're framed, we can see that we're dealing here not with the fleeting intelligence of man, but with something absolute, something eternal. Because in those three questions, the entire subsequent history of mankind is, as it were, gathered together into one whole and foretold in advance, and in them are united every unresolved contradiction of human nature. At the time it couldn't have been so clear, since the future was still unknown; but now that fifteen hundred years have passed, we can see that everything in those three questions was so rightly foreseen, so precisely foretold, and has come true so exactly, that nothing can be added to them, and nothing taken away.

"'Judge for Yourself who was right—You, or the one who questioned You then? Remember the first question; its meaning, put another way, was this: "You want to go out into the world, and You're going empty-handed, carrying nothing but some promise of freedom that men, in their simplicity and their natural unruliness, can't even understand, a freedom they fear and dread—because nothing has ever been more unbearable for a man, or for human society, than freedom. But do You see these stones, here in this parched and barren wilderness? Turn them into bread, and mankind will run after You like a flock of sheep, grateful and obedient, though forever trembling for fear You might withdraw Your hand and take back Your bread." But You wouldn't strip man of his freedom, and You rejected the offer, thinking: what is that freedom worth, if obedience has to be bought with bread? You answered that man does not live by bread alone. But do You know that for the sake of that earthly bread, the spirit of the earth will rise up against You, will fight You and defeat You, and everyone will follow him, crying out, "Who can compare to this beast? He has given us fire from heaven!" Do You know that the ages will pass, and humanity will proclaim, through the mouths of its wise men, that there is no such thing as crime, and therefore no sin—only hunger? "Feed men first, and then ask virtue of them!"—that's what they'll write on the banner they raise against You, the very banner with which they'll tear down Your temple. Where Your temple stood, a new building will rise; the terrible Tower of Babel will be built all over again, and though, like the first one, it will never be finished, still, You could have prevented that new tower, could have spared men a thousand years of suffering; because after a thousand years of agony with their tower, they'll come back to us all the same. They will seek us out again, hidden underground in the catacombs, because we will be persecuted and tortured all over again. They will find us, and cry out to us: "Feed us, because those who promised us fire from heaven never gave it!" And then we will finish building their tower for them, because it is the one who feeds them who finishes the building. And we alone will feed them in Your name, falsely claiming it is done in Your name. Oh, never, never will they be able to feed themselves without us! No science will ever give them bread as long as they remain free. In the end they will lay their freedom at our feet and say to us, "Make us your slaves, but feed us." They will understand, at last, that freedom and bread enough for everyone can never coexist, because they will never, ever manage to share it fairly among themselves! They will become convinced, too, that they can never truly be free, because they are weak, corrupt, worthless, and rebellious. You promised them the bread of Heaven, but I say again, can that possibly compare, in the eyes of the weak, the eternally sinful, the ignoble race of man, to earthly bread? And if, for the sake of the bread of Heaven, thousands follow You, what becomes of the millions, the tens of thousands of millions of souls who won't have the strength to give up earthly bread for the sake of heavenly bread? Or do You only care about the tens of thousands of the great and the strong, while the millions, countless as the sands of the sea, who are weak but love You, exist only to serve the great and the strong? No—we care for the weak too. They are sinful and rebellious, but in the end they too will become obedient. They will marvel at us, look on us as gods, because we are willing to bear the very freedom they found so terrifying, and rule over them instead—so dreadful will it seem to them, to be free. But we will tell them that we are Your servants, ruling in Your name. We will deceive them once again, because we will never let You come to us again. That deception will be our own suffering, because we will be forced to lie.

"'This is the meaning of the first question in the wilderness, and this is what You rejected, all for the sake of that freedom which You valued above everything else. And yet hidden inside that question lies the great secret of this world. Choosing "bread," You would have satisfied the universal, everlasting craving of humanity—to find someone to worship. As long as man remains free, nothing torments him and drives him more relentlessly than the search for someone to worship. But man doesn't just want something he alone can worship—he wants something established beyond all dispute, something everyone could agree at once to worship together. Because these pitiful creatures aren't only concerned with finding something one person or another can worship—they need to find something all of them can believe in and worship together; what matters above all is that they be together in it. This craving for a shared act of worship is the deepest misery of every man individually, and of all humanity, since the beginning of time. For the sake of shared worship, they've slaughtered each other with the sword. They've set up gods and challenged one another: "Cast aside your gods and come worship ours, or we will kill you and your gods too!" And so it will go on until the end of the world, even once gods have vanished from the earth entirely—men will still bow down before idols all the same. You knew, You had to have known, this fundamental secret of human nature, and yet You rejected the one infallible banner that was offered You, the one that would have made every man bow down to You alone—the banner of earthly bread; and You rejected it for the sake of freedom and the bread of Heaven. And look at what You did next. And again, all in the name of freedom! I tell You, nothing torments a man more than the anxiety of finding someone, quickly, to whom he can hand over that gift of freedom the poor creature was born with. But only someone who can set his conscience at rest can take that freedom from him. In bread, an unbeatable banner was offered You: give bread, and man will worship You, because nothing is more certain than bread. But if someone else gains control of his conscience—oh, then he will throw away Your bread and follow whoever has captured his conscience instead. In that, You were right. Because the secret of human existence isn't merely to live, but to have something to live for. Without a firm sense of what he's living for, a man won't consent to go on living at all, and would sooner destroy himself than stay on this earth, even surrounded by bread. That much is true. But what happened instead? Instead of taking men's freedom away from them, You made it greater than ever! Did You forget that man would rather have peace, even death, than freedom to choose between good and evil? Nothing seduces a man more than freedom of conscience, but nothing causes him greater suffering either. And look what You did: instead of giving men something solid to rest their conscience on forever, You chose everything that was exceptional, vague, and enigmatic; You chose things that lay entirely beyond human strength, acting as though You didn't love them at all—You, who came to give Your very life for them! Instead of taking hold of men's freedom, You expanded it, and burdened the spiritual kingdom of mankind with its agonies forever. You wanted man's free love, wanted him to follow You freely, drawn and captivated by You of his own will. In place of the old, rigid law, man would now have to decide for himself, freely, what is good and what is evil, with only Your image before him as a guide. But didn't You know that in the end he would reject even Your image, even Your truth, once he was crushed under the terrible weight of free choice? They will cry out at last that the truth isn't in You at all, because they could never have been left in greater confusion and suffering than what You caused them, burdening them with so many cares, so many unanswerable questions.

"'So that, in truth, it was You Yourself who laid the foundation for the destruction of Your own kingdom, and no one else bears more of the blame for it. And yet what was offered to You? There are three powers, only three, capable of conquering and holding forever captive the conscience of these weak rebels, for their own happiness—those forces are miracle, mystery, and authority. You rejected all three, and set the example for rejecting them. When the wise and dread spirit set You on the pinnacle of the temple and said to You, "If You want to know whether You are the Son of God, then cast Yourself down, for it is written: the angels shall bear Him up, lest He fall and hurt Himself, and then You will know whether You are truly the Son of God, and will prove then how great Your faith in Your Father is." But You refused, and would not cast Yourself down. Oh, of course, You acted with pride and with dignity, as befits God; but the weak, unruly race of men—are they gods? Oh, You knew even then that in taking one step, in making even one motion to throw Yourself down, You would be tempting God and would have lost all faith in Him, and would have been dashed to pieces on the very earth You came to save. And the wise spirit who tempted You would have rejoiced. But I ask again: are there many like You? Could You seriously believe, even for a moment, that men too could withstand a temptation like that? Is human nature really such that it can reject miracle, and at the great moments of life, the moments of its deepest, most agonizing spiritual struggle, cling only to the free verdict of the heart? Oh, You knew Your deed would be written into books, passed down through distant ages to the furthest ends of the earth, and You hoped that man, following Your example, would cling to God without demanding a miracle. But You didn't know that when man rejects miracle, he rejects God along with it; because man doesn't search so much for God as for the miraculous. And since man can't bear to live without the miraculous, he will go and invent new miracles of his own, and will worship deeds of sorcery and witchcraft, even if he's a rebel, a heretic, and an unbeliever a hundred times over. You didn't come down from the cross when they shouted up at You, mocking and jeering, "Come down from the cross and we will believe that it is You." You didn't come down, because once again You refused to enslave man through a miracle, and craved a faith freely given, not one built on miracle. You craved free love, not the base raptures of a slave forever cowering before a power that has crushed him into submission. But in that, You thought too highly of men, because they are slaves, of course, however rebellious by nature. Look around and judge for Yourself; fifteen centuries have passed—look at them now. Whom have You managed to raise up to Yourself? I swear, man is weaker and baser by nature than You ever believed him to be! Can he, can he possibly do what You did? By showing him so much respect, You stopped, in a sense, feeling for him at all, because You asked far too much of him—You, who loved him more than You loved Yourself! Had You respected him less, You would have asked less of him. That would have been closer to love, because his burden would have been lighter. He is weak and vile. What does it matter that he's now rebelling everywhere against our authority, proud of his own rebellion? It's the pride of a child, a schoolboy. They're small children, rioting, locking the teacher out of the classroom. But their childish glee will come to an end; it will cost them dearly. They will tear down temples and soak the earth in blood. But eventually they'll see, these foolish children, that although they are rebels, they are powerless rebels, unable even to sustain their own rebellion. Drowning in their own foolish tears, they will finally recognize that He who made them rebels must have meant to mock them. They will say this in despair, and the saying of it will be a blasphemy that will make them even more miserable still, because human nature cannot bear blasphemy, and always, in the end, avenges it on itself. And so unrest, confusion, and misery—that is man's present lot, after You bore so much for the sake of his freedom! The great prophet describes, in vision and image, seeing all those who took part in the first resurrection, twelve thousand from each tribe. But if there were that many of them, they couldn't have been men—they must have been gods. They had carried Your cross, endured decades in the barren, starving wilderness, living on locusts and roots—and You may indeed point to them with pride, these children of freedom, of free love, of free and glorious sacrifice made in Your name. But remember, there were only a few thousand of them; and what of the rest? How are the other weak ones to blame, for failing to endure what the strong endured? How is a weak soul to blame for being unable to receive such terrible gifts? Can it really be that You came only for the elect, and only to the elect? If so, then it is a mystery, and we cannot understand it. And if it is a mystery, then we too have the right to preach a mystery, and to teach men that what matters isn't the free judgment of their hearts, isn't love, but a mystery they must follow blindly, even against their own conscience. And that is exactly what we have done. We have corrected Your work, and have built it instead on miracle, mystery, and authority. And men rejoiced that they were once again being led like sheep, that the terrible gift which had caused them such suffering was finally lifted from their hearts. Were we right to teach them this? Speak! Did we not love mankind, in so meekly acknowledging their weakness, so lovingly lightening their burden, permitting their feeble nature even to sin, with our blessing? Why have You come now to stand in our way? And why do You look at me so silently, so searchingly, with those gentle eyes? Be angry instead. I don't want Your love, because I do not love You.
